speechtext:
Order, please. Yesterday the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), at the conclusion of the question period, raised a point of order concerning the alleged reference to a document by the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) during that question period. The purpose of the point of order was that within the regulations and precedents in our practice the minister, having made reference to that document or having cited the document, ought to be compelled by the House to produce it.
There are three aspects to the matter. The first is whether the minister, in terms of the precedents, in fact cited the document. In that respect I would refer the House to a ruling by Mr. Speaker Lamoureux on November 16, 1971, which reads as follows:
In fairness, looking at the matter as objectively as I can, I do not see how it is possible for the Chair to make a ruling at this point that a document that has simply been referred to but has not been directly quoted should be tabled in debate. I find it difficult to rule otherwise, Hon. members may look at the citations that have been quoted in a very interesting and forceful way by the hon. members ... If a document has been actually cited or quoted in debate by a minister of the Crown, it has to be tabled. If only reference is made to it, I do not see how there can be an obligation to table it.
The interpretation of that precedent ought to be strict where the document has first been referred to in the question period by a questioner. It ought to be interpreted much more against the minister, in my opinion, if-as the rule and the precedent
80008-1iVi

Privilege-Mr. Oberle
envisage-a minister is in a situation where in debate, which is what the rule says, the minister has taken an advantage of the rest of the House by referring to, citing or quoting a document in his possession but not in the possession of the rest of. the House.
Therefore, if in the question period-which strictly speaking, is not debate but has some parallel application-a minister were to make first reference to a document, which gave him an advantage in answering a question, that the rest of the House did not have in pursuing further questions, the rule could be interpreted in that way. However, where the document is raised and, in answer, some reference is made by a minister, the language of Mr. Speaker Lamoureux is directly applicable: there would have to be a direct quotation or citation, which was not the case yesterday.
In any case, there are two other aspects to the matter. Second, there seems to be some desire on the part of those pressing for the production of the document that some altered form of the document be produced. Surely it would not be expected that this House, or the Chair especially, would formulate an order which would tell a minister to produce a document in response to that order-not the entire document but merely an expurgated version. I have the greatest difficulty understanding how such an order could be phrased and, therefore, I am not prepared to proceed with it.
In the final analysis, the minister claims that the document ought not to be released by him in respect of the public interest. It is conceded, certainly, by both the arguments, specifically by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the action of the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) in support of his point of order, that by leaving out large portions of the document it would, in fact, be against the public interest to table the entire document. Therefore, for those three reasons I will not order the document to be produced.

speechtext:

speechtext: Having given the Chair the proper notice, Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand, to move the adjournment of the House under the terms of Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and urgent matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the failure of the Prime Minister to tell the House and the Canadian people what steps he proposes to take to counter the threat to Canadian confederation posed by the separatist government in Quebec. This question must be transferred from the public arena to its proper place, the chamber of the House of Commons, where it can be debated by the representatives of all the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext:
The hon. member gave the Chair notice, pursuant to Standing Order 26, of his intention to raise this matter. He has put forward a motion which relates to three questions. One has to do with a threat to Canadian confederation; second, the election of a separatist government in Quebec; and, third, the failure of the Prime Minister to inform the House-if I may quote from the motion-what steps he proposes to take to counter the threat to confederation, and so on. With regard to the first two questions, subparagraph (16) of Standing Order 26 reads as follows:
The right to move the adjournment of the House for the above purposes is subject to the following conditions:
(a) the matter proposed for discussion must relate to a genuine emergency
calling for immediate and urgent consideration-
I interpret that language as meaning that an order for debate cannot proceed if the subject suggested, however important or pressing, does not constitute an emergency but is a matter of a continuing nature. The motion expresses an opinion-and I stress that it is the hon. member's opinion- that the result of the Quebec election constitutes a threat to

confederation. But the hon. member must surely realize that if it is a threat to confederation, it is a continuing threat and not one of an emergency nature as envisaged in subsection (a) of section 16 of the Standing Order. Therefore, I would refrain from granting the special debate pursuant to Standing Order 26 on that basis. Furthermore, I am most reluctant to enter into an expression of opinion as to whether or not an election that has taken place in any province, being a duly lawful and proper election within the procedures known under our system, can, as an opinion of the Chair, constitute what is required by the Standing Order to be an emergency calling for immediate and urgent consideration.
In the final analysis, the hon. member moves from those two points to concentrate in the motion on the failure of the Prime Minister to tell this House what steps he is taking to counteract the results of this election. In that respect, while I would not say so except with the very greatest reluctance, since that is a criticism of the Prime Minister I would have to consider, under section (5) of the Standing Order, whether that is a very proper use of the allotted days that will be following.
I am very reluctant to use the escape under Standing Order 26 that so long as an opposition day remains there is a chance to discuss matters of importance, and therefore the rule ought not to be used to set up a debate. Standing Order 26 was changed in order, I think, to remove debate on whether or not the order should go, and to set up hours that could be used by the Chair which are auxiliary hours to the regular sittings. I think those changes were made in order to see that matters of national importance which ought to be debated in this chamber and which would not likely be debated in other ways could be debated under the application of the order.
I do not like to refute that by saying that since an opposition day may be coming up, that notice ought to be taken. I think that forces upon the opposition an obligation which is not natural with respect to the use of those days. However, that part of the hon. member's motion which seeks to criticize the Prime Minister for his failure to make a disclosure to this House seems to me to be a very proper use of one of the opposition days. Therefore, having regard to the two reasons that I cited previously relative to subsection (16)(a), and for the latter reason relative to section (5) of the rule, I do not see fit to set aside special hours pursuant to Standing Order 26 to debate the motion put forward by the hon. member.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Wednesday, January 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien that Bill C-23, to facilitate conversion to the metric system of measurement, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I conclude my remarks I should like to correct a portion of my remarks appearing in Hansard for yesterday at page 2429. I am reported as having said: "No matter how you look at it, there is no benefit to the manufacturer." I thought I said: "No matter how you look at it, there will only be benefit to the manufacturer." That was one of the points I was trying to make. As a result of the insistence of the manufacturers, without thought for all other segments of the economy, we are being forced into a system without any consultation. It is a common complaint among farmers that they are being saddled with costs and the buck stops there, as it is often said: they are at the mercy of prices over which they have no control.
It is quite evident from the remarks made by other members from western Canada that the readings we have been getting from our constituencies and from people with whom we have been in contact the last little while are entirely different from those that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) has apparently been getting, or wants to lead us to believe he has been getting.
I referred to the confusion and to the case of a man trying to get directions. Present-day roads will be in existence for years to come and will be measured in terms of miles, not kilometres. Speedometers or mileage meters will be calibrated in kilometres; therefore you will not be able to give specific directions in years to come. Under the new system people will be bamboozled for years to come. In fact, we will be using two systems. That in itself will complicate matters.
The fact is, as other people have said, that this change will not produce one bushel more. In fact, it will only add to total cost; it will add nothing to efficiency. Replacement parts for many machines will no longer be available. I know for a fact, from past experience, that machinery companies practice planned obsolescence; they do not intend to manufacture any item to last longer than they feel is necessary. They are the ones who make the decisions. As I pointed out yesterday, you cannot even replace a simple thing like a rim by using one from another machine; you have to buy the rim made for the machine. On our farm I believe at the last count there were like 115 to 120 tires around the place, so one can imagine the number of rims required. I am sure other farms have more, or perhaps less, but the fact is that in many instances these rims are not interchangeable.
Metric System
Manufacturers keep insisting that if they are more competitive and can break into world markets, their cost of production will go down. If it is good business for them to standardize in terms of the rest of the world, then we as consumers should demand of the minister-and he might consider this-that legislation should be brought forward to compel manufacturers to give us something in return. I should like to see the minister come forward and insist that manufacturers standardize on items such as chains, bearings, sprockets, and so on. These items differ in size by a fraction of an inch, which means that one rim will not fit over another hub. This is a deliberate attempt on the part of manufacturers to make you buy their parts only, and there is no need for that. There should be standardization. If we are expected to pay the price of this conversion, surely we should expect something from the manufacturers. Therefore, I would ask the minister seriously to consider whether he can compel these manufacturers to standardize.
For example, why is it that a car cannot use the same type of windshield over a number of different model years? Instead, the manufacturer adds a fraction of an inch, or makes it slightly smaller, or gives it a little more curvature so that it cannot be used in a car of a different year should it need replacement. As far as I am concerned, this would help keep down the fires of inflation. Certainly it would reduce costs in many areas.
In many instances people are struggling for survival, as are many operations. We witness this day in and day out. Many people are not fussy about the newness of a given piece of equipment or instrument; they are more concerned about its serviceability. This is particularly true of trucks. Many farmers use trucks, but in this regard they do not get the co-operation from the manufacturer which the manufacturer expects from the consumer, particularly in the agricultural field. Several pelleting plants in my constituency sell their product to Japan. They tell me they never had any difficulty selling their pellets to Japan under the old system. If Japan wanted quantities in metric tonnes, they could comply with that request. There has never been any confusion. So why in the world are we suddenly faced with this Latin conversion which will simply add to the total cost, and in many instances, will add unnecessarily to the existing confusion? It will add to the cost as a result of delay and inefficiency.
It is bad enough for the farmer to have to sit down and make the calculations, but if he sends his man out into the field on the machinery, you can imagine how much attention that man will pay to proper measurement. I have had some experience along this line, and let me assure you that I have had to re-seed quite a few acres in rapeseed because the proper calculations were not made. I suggest this new system of measurement will only add to the total cost of operations. There will, no doubt, be additional confusion, and perhaps that is why a request I have heard often is being made by people who have considered this matter. The suggestion is that we adopt an interim measurement so that between the time we

It might be easy for the farmer to double-check on these calculations during the winter months, but from the time of winter break-up to the first snow, farmers are too busy to take time off to check measurements, calculations and payments for the various grades they have sold.
I appeal to the minister to set up a system to monitor pricing in retail outlets. I mentioned the incident involving the shaving cream with three different measurements and three different prices. We cannot expect everyone to carry a calculator. If we did, we would be like a bunch of robots. However, the department should involve itself in this problem. If there is a price increase that is too high, an inspector might usefully spend some time checking the price in various outlets. This would be appreciated not only by housewives but by consumers. In the case of coffee, sugar and almost anything else, many retail outlets have taken advantage of any change to increase the price, which never again comes down.
I conclude, Mr. Speaker, by assuring the House that the farming community is not enthusiastic about this change. We feel it will add to confusion, with absolutely no benefit.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it odd to speak now on this bill on metric conversion, because I had the opportunity to speak on the subject when the bill was originally introduced in the House a number of years ago. The hon. member just mentioned one problem which we experience as the result of a conglomeration of sizes of parts for farm machinery and implements. We all know about coarse threads, fine threads, various pitch threads, metric threads, standard threads, pipe threads and others. Obviously, it is an expensive proposition for the farmer to maintain a supply of parts for his equipment in order to make normal repairs. One reason I am in favour of going to the metric system is to eliminate the problems we have as a result of these various sizes. By adopting the metric system we would standardize things such as nuts and bolts.
[Mr. Korchinski.J
I have in the past often found that when you ask a civil servant to do something, he quite often does not do what you ask, or does something that goes beyond what is required or is in any way advantageous to you. In fact, very often the civil servant creates more problems. Having regard to what the last speaker said in respect of standardization, one of the problems farmers are now experiencing has been expressed by wheat pools, farm organizations and others. They have suggested that unless civil servants pay attention to the needs of the consumer, the consumer will be ripped off to an extent never before experienced. The rip-off already exists to a degree or we would not have this suggestion to simplify the complex problem involving measurement. In simplifying the problem we may be encouraging a rip-off against the farmer.
Let us consider tire sizes for a moment. Considering the number of changes that have been made in the last ten years, it is a wonder that anyone can buy replacement tires for his automobile, truck or tractor. If the change continues, soon we will not be able to buy tires that will fit our rims. Perhaps we will require two sizes, one to fit the rims that originally came with the car, and one as a replacement size. This is only an example; there are many things like this. There is a tremendous opportunity for the government to prevent this rip-off by industry in respect of size changes. Let me give the example of the antique car. If you want parts, you must have them manufactured specifically for the automobile, at tremendous cost.
Let me refer to the propaganda put out by the minister respecting the agricultural industry going metric. It starts out by suggesting that in 1977 Canada and the United States will be converting to the metric measurement system used by the rest of the world. That is a lot of bull; it is not true. The rest of the world never used this system, and in this respect the government is being totally dishonest. What happened was that many countries got together and established a metric unit of measurement. For years Italy, France and many European countries have used the metric system in respect of temperature. We have developed a new international metric unit of measurement for temperature, and we are doing this in a number of other areas. We are not accepting the system that was in use in other countries, and I think people should be told that. What we are doing-and we have no objection to it-is embarking upon a world measurement system that is expressed in metric units. This will apply to countries which have been on the metric system even more than it will apply to this country.
People who thought they were talking about degrees of Centigrade in terms of temperature now find they are talking in terms of degrees of Celsius, which is a totally new unit applied internationally to the measurement of temperature. The Centigrade measurement was retained for the radius of a circle because the radius of a circle and temperature have no relationship to each other. The same is true of Pascal in the measurement of pressure, and many other things. There were obviously many units of metric measurement in use through-

January 27, 1977
out the world which were not the same as other units. We have designed new international units of metric measurement which all countries of the world have agreed to adopt. I do not think the government is aware of the criticism it is going to receive. It is saying that the farmer will have to change.
Mr. Speaker, I decided I was going to learn the Celsius scale and know what it was all about. When I looked at the barometer and saw it was 10 degrees below zero, however, I could not decide whether it was cold or was not cold. When I got outside I found I was wearing too many clothes, because the barometer was reading Celsius. After two years of looking at the stupid barometer I bought one that had both Fahrenheit and Celsius on it. Then I would listen to the radio to find out the temperature, and look out the window at my barometer to see what it said, and between them I could work out how cold it was.
In this country we have encountered a lot of problems with the introduction of bilingualism, but I do not think any of us would say that we were wrong in passing the Official Languages Act. It is a different thing, however, when it is implemented and John Doe is told that he has to become bilingual. I have only to recall my own difficulties with Celsius to realize how difficult it is for him. Now we are telling industry that it is to their advantage to make the conversion to metric.
Mr. Speaker, I do not have much sympathy with any difficulties the Canadian Wheat Board may encounter or any problems that may develop for the wheat pools. For the benefit of the parliamentary secretary, may I say that I am informed it will cost $400,000 or $500,000 for the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool to convert. When we start talking about the farmer going over to hectares and kilograms, however, I can foresee a great deal of unfavourable reaction.
I think it would have been possible for the government to have asked industry to label products with the old and the new measurements. In my opinion it is not necessary for the farmer to make the conversion. He can look over his 40 acres, but I do not think it is necessary for him to know that it is 13 or 14 hectares. To him it is a 40-acre field and he knows he is going to get 15 bushels to the acre from that field. When he takes the grain to the elevator, they will tell him the quantity in tonnes. In some of the publications sent to farmers there appears the sentence, "Your truck may hold tonnes". I suppose it depends on the size of the truck, but when he takes the grain to the elevator they will tell him how many tonnes there are.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) pointed out the legal problems involved in changing the basis of land measurement. It will affect all the deeds in existence. Acres will have to be translated into hectares. Mr. Speaker, I do not think that is necessary and, indeed, I do not think it will happen. When the farmer gets an invoice from the elevator, the amount will be expressed in tonnes, and when he gets the invoice for his milk it will be expressed in litres. Packages are now labelled in both French and English. Maybe it would be better not to have the English, because in that way we would quickly pick up a knowledge of French.
Metric System
I know I can always find my way to the washroom no matter what language it is in. Indeed, in some of the airports they use symbols and you do not even need to know the language. The farmer would be assisted if there were a translation to metric on labels. Then he would not have to make the conversion himself. In one generation of teaching children the metric system, the conversion will be made, and I have no objection to that. What I object to, and what I think the farmer objects to, is the demand that he make the conversion himself. I do not think that is necessary. Civil servants see this as a simple problem, as they saw the two official languages as a simple problem. They said that everybody would speak both languages, but now they find that even they are having trouble mastering the second language. The average person will still function in the way that is easiest. The distance from the floor to the ceiling is still approximately eight feet, and when you get a two by four we all know what it is: no matter what the new equivalent may be called, to most of us it will still be a two by four.
It may be important to the industry what the new measurement is but it is not important to me. The wall is still going to be a certain thickness no matter how thick the studs are. The farmer will be required to make the conversion in the amount of grain he sows, the amount of fertilizer he uses and the amount of land he owns. He will not convert to metric terms but, rather, back to the terms with which he is familiar. Therefore, I suggest that the government should be very careful about forcing anyone to make these changes.
In this booklet we are told to go out and buy a 10-metre and 30-metre tape. What for? Farmers will build their buildings as long, or as wide, as they want them, no matter what the tape is. They understand how long they want their building to be, and they can do that with the old tape: they will not buy a new one.
I suggest that the conversion should be gradual, and it will be done successfully if we do not force it, if we do not demand that people become confused. There is no reason for the elevator not to use the two systems, because the elevator people have the assistance of a computer. The next generation will learn the metric system in school, and those who are not familiar with the metric system and are not able to learn it should be allowed to use the system which they know; and even if fractions occur it will not concern them very much in calculating bulk shipments.
I have been very interested to read that by such and such a date the conversion must take place, or that such and such is the earliest completion date, or that the absolute completion date must be before such a period, and so on. Why is that? I do not know why it has to be. Perhaps the minister can explain why in some areas conversion must take place by a certain date. We have not used the metric system in this country previously, yet our grain sales to international markets were made under the metric system simply because that was the way it was done. It did not bother anyone shipping grain that

January 27, 1977
Metric System
that was the way it was done. This was done by computer, and I suppose they assumed that if the computer would accept it, everyone in the country would do the same. However, I am scared they will not.
I would like this conversion to take place as quickly as possible and with as little difficulty as possible, but we must not insist on these changes being made. There was no need to rush, in my opinion, to convert the dairy industry to the metric system. I spoke to some of the dairymen and they told me that when they put out their new containers they had to record a lot of information on them. Then they were refused a licence because in the next stage of the process they had to add some more information. It did not make any difference to the consumer who knew what a quart was and who did not care how it was processed through the machines. It is this kind of insistence on conversion by a certain date that, I am sure, has created some unnecessary expense that could have been avoided quite easily.
So I express the hope, as a practical politician-which most of us here are-that if the civil servants have done a good job, part of their job will be to explain to the people here the necessity of using the new metric units which are used in the international community. Their second responsibility is also a big one. If you take all the quarts of milk off the shelf and replace them with litres, I am not sure whether they will be bigger or smaller. If the housewife does not know whether it is bigger or smaller and wants to know whether she is paying the same amount for the milk, the government has the responsibility to police the pricing so that she does not get gouged in the changeover. This also goes for farm machinery. If we find that a new machine becomes obsolete in two years because, due to the conversion to the metric system, the wheels or the tires cannot be replaced, the public will feel gypped.
The minister and the civil servants have a responsibility to set up an enforcement branch in the department which will ensure that we do not get short-changed when the conversion is made. If a product is smaller, shorter or lighter, we will not know whether we are paying too much or too little for that commodity, because of the change. Unless we know that, we will feel cheated. In fact, we already think we are. So it seems to me that it is the responsibility of the minister and his department to police this matter for us until the conversion is completed.
I do not think it matters a hoot whether it is a bushel, a kilogram or a ton. A farmer looked at a bag and he knew that if he had wheat in it, it was heavier than if he had oats. If he looked in the bin, he knew there would be so many bags in it. In western Canada they look in the bin and they say it will cost so much when it goes to the elevator. The farmer was used to that, he was familiar with what was there, and it will not matter to him whether we have converted to the metric system unless only the new measurements are put on the bin, measurements with which he is not familiar so he will not know whether he is overpaying. If he thinks he is, the government will never sell that system to him.
(Mr. Peters.]
In certain areas the conversion does not have to be pushed quickly. There should be no turning back from the metric system, but I am concerned that we in Canada are trying to show the United States that we are better and faster at converting than they are. The backlash against the government and the Liberal party will not be too bad in western Canada because it will affect only a couple of members, but at the least it will produce a heck of a lot noise, and it may affect some of us in eastern Canada as well. We do not need to be the showplace of the North American continent in metric conversion. Let us proceed with it as fast as acceptable.
I am very interested in hearing what the minister has to say about policing the changes that are made, so that there is no rip-off. It is evident that there could be rip-offs in replacement parts of equipment. Some increased costs may be justified, but it is the minister's responsibility to ensure that there are no rip-offs. I hope he can tell us that a number of people in his department will be continually policing what is being done in industry to protect the consumer after the conversion.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to Bill C-23 I, too, wish to register some criticisms and concerns about conversion to the metric system on behalf of the people I represent in the Pembina constituency. In spite of the fact that one might be in basic agreement with the position that Canada should join most other peoples in the world in establishing a unified system of measurement, there are, nevertheless, a number of concerns which deserve comment and study. There can be no doubt about the fact that such an important change will be the stimulus of much frustration during the transition period. While some Canadians will be hurt more than others by the conversion to the metric system, eventually all will be affected by way of increased costs to consumers in the form of increased prices. The exact impact remains an unknown quantity, but it is certain to contribute to an already serious inflationary problem. There have been no estimates of the cost, but in the United States conversion cost estimates range from $40 billion to $100 billion. At the usual one-tenth differential between Americans and Canadians, that means between $4 billion and $10 billion for Canada.
Many small firms may be faced with undue expenses in adapting to the metric system. Added costs will affect their competitive status and may disrupt profits for a year or two. There is the added possibility of business failure in some cases. Although the metrication process is not as far advanced in the United States as it is here, a U.S. Senate bill on metrication was introduced on January 15, 1975, with provisions specifically designed to help small businesses. The bill would enable the administration, in consultation with the secretary of commerce, to make loans to them either directly or in co-operation with banks or other lending institutions through agreement to enable them to participate on an immediate or deferred basis. The American bill would also authorize the small business administration-a U.S. government agency which provides business loans-to make grants to individuals to defray non-
January 27, 1977

reimbursable expenses for tools, and so forth, to a maximum of $2,000 per person. It is suggested that we introduce an amendment along these lines.
The guiding financial principle of this government is to let the costs lie where they fall. This is regarded by many groups, manufacturing concerns and individuals, as being most inequitable. It is not in the national interest for some groups to suffer while others benefit under a policy which is supposed to serve the long-term good of all Canadians.
In a good many ways this debate is useless because the government, in its 1970 white paper on metric conversion, committed Canada to converting from the current inches-pounds system of measurement to the international system based on metric units. However useless this debate may be, we as members of parliament have an obligation to register our protest on behalf of those we represent. Who will this measure benefit? One thing is for sure; it will not benefit the farmers of this country.
Comments have already been made by other speakers about the tremendous cost of conversion to the metric system and the disruption of changing from acres to hectares and changing the traditional ways of the farmers who have been brought up to know certain measurements. All these things have become part of the culture of our people. This sudden change hits our farmers first. I cannot understand the rationale behind this change. The government states it is because our commodities are sold on the world markets and that most of our trading partners use the metric system. I suggest that the point of export is where we should make the conversion to the metric system, and not at the farm level.
The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski), the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk), the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) have all expressed reservations about converting to the metric system. They have done a superb job in this debate expressing the views of our western farmers. So rather than prolong this debate, let me close by expressing my hope that this measure will be given further thought and that the minister will give serious consideration to the realistic proposals made by the hon. members I just mentioned.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will limit my observations to the part of this bill dealing with prairie agriculture and with the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, and point out the much more serious and far-reaching implications which might not occur to most people involved in the changeover.
When considering adopting the metric system, it would be helpful to think about how our present system came about. Originally, a yard was the length of a man's arm, or to use a more modern phrase, the length of a person's arm. When people related the distance of a yard in their own minds they could at least look at their arm to assess how long it was. But
Metric System
what is a metre? If my memory serves me correctly, the length of the metre was decided by Napoleon and the standard measurement is in some Paris institution. I do not know whether it is on public view, but it is something most of us have never seen and very few will ever see. To us the yard represents something which is tangible; it is approximately the length of a person's arm.
It might be convenient to some to use a kilogram, which is something like 2.2 pounds, or a ton, but a ton is far too big for an individual to estimate properly. A bushel was something a man could carry. He could visualize a bushel basket, but could he visualize the equivalent in metric terms? Of course not! We have ten kilograms, 20 kilograms or 30 kilograms, and we end up with a ton, which is approximately 60 bushels of wheat or 70 bushels of barley. It cannot be visualized. The metric system is a fine thing for large grain companies when they handle boxcars, shiploads or unit trains of grain. The ton is a workable unit for them, but it is rather ridiculous for the government to argue that we need a changeover to sell our grain. We have been selling it metrically for decades in the world markets.
It is interesting that the people who agree with this change are the grain handling companies, of which there are just a few. As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) said, it would be fine in air-conditioned offices where there are computers to deal with the metric system, but the farmer out on his windy acres with the rain pouring, or with dust in his eyes, would find it difficult to use the metric system. It is not easy to use the metric system at the farm level because there are certain inherent problems. This part of the bill deals with western Canada, and western Canada was surveyed on the mile square or the one mile by two miles square. Everyone knows that a section is 640 acres, more or less, depending on corrections necessary for latitude and longitude. A quarter section is 160 acres. An acre is something we can visualize, but with this bill we would have hectares, which bears no relationship to anything. If this bill could make two plants grow where only one grew before, it might make some sense; but obviously agricultural land does not get any bigger just because we change from acres to hectares.
The ton measure is just too large for most farmers to understand. When I look at daily grain prices, I look at Chicago prices which are still quoted in bushels. Canadian prices are quoted in tons. The one ton price may be $289, whereas the bushel price may be $7, which is easily understood. To those accustomed to small measures, the ton is far too large a unit. This is one of the great difficulties with this metric system at the farm. In the grain trade you have several large companies staffed with competent people. These companies are different from the grain growers, and to the 200,000 permit-holders this is an entirely new system of measuring, a system to which producers will not easily adapt. The new system will come into common use somewhere down the road, but not without trouble. I contend that there is a serious possibility of loss of production. Certainly, the new system will not lead to any increase in production, and there is the distinct

January 27, 1977
Metric System
possibility of loss of production unless certain changes are made in accordance with the representations of the farming industry.
I hope, first, that the term "hectare" will be dropped and "acre" retained. There is no valid reason for not doing this, and it makes sense. Why can we not retain the measurements by "bushel"? The proposed system in this regard makes no sense. For example, the grain elevator agent who must deal with many farmers waiting to unload their grain will need to do much juggling with figures, looking up tables, and so on. He will buy by the ton, then measure the amount of grain loaded on the tank car, or boxcar, in bushels, because the grain transport system for a number of years to come will continue to use the bushel as a unit of measure. I understand it does not yet plan to change over to the metric system.
However, when the grain arrives at the other end of the line it will be measured according to a metric scale. Why cannot the grain continue to be bought in bushels so the elevator agent can continue to ship it in bushels? If the conversion to the metric measure must be made, why cannot it be made at the higher level, so to speak-the other end of the line?
Civil servants who planned this bill have not thought through its full effects. For example, how will the farmer learn to measure his new volumes of fertilizer and herbicide? Herbicides in spray form are applied in small volume. You are dealing with small units, say two or three ounces in ten gallons of water per acre, or perhaps up to 16 ounces of herbicide in 20 gallons of water per acre. It is all too easy to make a mistake in the application of herbicide. If they are applied too thinly, money is wasted because the herbicides will not do the job; but if more than the required amount is applied, your crop is ruined. Many crops have been lost through the overapplication of herbicides. The question of fertilizer volumes is also important.
How are farm implements to be altered? Drills are governed by acre meters, not hectare meters. These drills are mostly American-made. American manufacturers dominate the market and we can expect such drills to remain on the market for a long time. How can a farmer calculate how much seed or fertilizer he must use? He will buy his fertilizer, presumably, by the kilogram and then calculate how much his drill, which will be governed by acre meter, will require for a given area.
It is useless telling the farmer to get a hectare meter; he will not do it. As I have said, 90 per cent of drills are American-made, not Canadian-made. So far as I know, only one company in this country makes drills, Co-op Implements. Therefore, you will not see many metric drills in western Canada or eastern Canada until they are made in the United States, because the farm implement business is really continentwide. It is important to recognize this. For example, at present seed drills come with six-inch, seven-inch and eight-inch runs; I suppose they come in other sizes too. We will not get equivalent drills set up in centimetres, say with 2.5 centimetres being the equivalent of one inch. You will not see a 15-centimetre,

17.5 centimetre or 20 centimetre drill. Drill sizes will still be measured in inches because the North American market as a whole will still demand drills calibrated in inches, at least until the whole of this continent changes over to the metric system.
We send across the border much seed grain, including seed wheat, seed barley and forage seeds. The Department of Agriculture is anxious to increase our exports of forage seeds to the United States market; it is a good market for our clovers and legumes. But passage of this bill may help diminish our United States market because we shall export our seeds in bags labelled in kilograms. The American farmer buying our seed will not be happy. All other things being equal, he will buy the bag of seed labelled in units of measurement with which he is familiar. Therefore, passage of this bill could erect a trade barrier to exports to the United States market, the market to which we export most of our grain seed.
In essence, therefore, the proposed changeover has considerable potential for harm to production. Perhaps the damage will be impossible to measure. In any event, this bill will not in any way lead to increases in production. As I have said, it has a potential for decreasing production. Potentially, it could hurt the farm machinery industry, particularly of western Canada. I am referring to that part of the industry which sells machinery in the United States market. It is well known that up to 80 per cent of farm machinery produced in western Canada is sold on the American market. Therefore, that part of the industry must stay in tune with the American market and do what that market wants, not what civil servants in this country and the metric commission want.
This legislation will also make it difficult for farmers to calculate how much they are getting for their grain or produce. The farmer has been used to selling a bushel of grain, say for $3, a bushel of barley for $2, flax for $7 and rapeseed for $6. Some look on this bill as a conspiracy on the part of the grain industry to confuse the farmer because he will now be dealing with tons of grain. He will get so much money for each ton of grain; and one ton represents roughly the equivalent of 60 bushels. Certainly, the new system will make it more difficult for the farmer to know, on a day to day basis, if he is getting more, or less, for his grain or other produce. Therefore, the new system will bring only confusion to the 200,000 permit holders of western Canada.
It makes no sense to change the survey system from acres to hectares. So long as the grain transportation system uses the bushel as a measurement, grain should be measured in bushels. As an elevator agent told me, he must buy grain by the ton, then ship it by the bushel. He thought the system was stupid and that we were no further ahead. He said that the new system would only create more mistakes and there would be more difficulty all along the line.
Perhaps this legislation is the government's answer to unemployment. We shall need to employ more people to convert measurements from one system to another. However, until the transport system involving the hauling of grain changes over to the metric system, much of this legislation makes no sense. I am alluding to the problems of producers, the way elevator

agents will buy the grain and ship it. Surely it makes no sense to buy by the ton and then ship by the bushel. Remember, relatively unsophisticated people will be doing the measuring in a cold, windy elevator. The agent will buy by the ton, then turn around and ship the grain out by the bushel because the transportation system will still use that unit of measurement.
Surely the railroads of this country are better able to cope with the metric system than the individual farmer. Until they do, it is surely not the time for change. I repeat that in order to be uniform, somewhere down the road we will no doubt change to the metric system. There are many disadvantages to the metric system that we will only realize as we begin to use it. However, change for the sake of getting ahead of the Americans in the agricultural field does not make much sense through this aspect of the legislation.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 listened with interest yesterday to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) when he spoke in this debate. If you refer to Hansard you will note that at page 2422 he had this to say:
First, it should be noted that this change has a broad and virtually unanimous base of support in the farm community.
He later said:
I did not find the degree of antagonism which they perhaps see, or perhaps it would be more proper to say that they would like to see and would like to foment.
In the latter quote he is referring to the members of the opposition. I did not find that type of support in my constituency. The support was far from unanimous. If I repeated in this House some of the remarks made to me by farmers, Your Honour would undoubtedly call me out of order. The hon. member stated that members of this party were trying to foment antagonism with the farmers in connection with this bill. If there is any antagonism on the part of the farmer, that antagonism has been caused by the present government with its LIFT program, cheap barley sales and failure to appreciate the problems of the livestock industry in western Canada.
The hon. member for Assiniboia also indicated that there was considerable saving to be made by converting to the metric system. As reported at page 2423 of Hansard, he said:
I want to deal, as well, with the question of cost, which has been mentioned, or more particularly with cost savings. A lot of people have been skeptical about the matter. In response to that skepticism I have asked the committee of the Grains Council to demonstrate clearly where the cost savings are, and it has produced a detailed analysis which indicates an annual saving to the grains industry in the order of $1 million.
That is an interesting statement, but the hon. member did not produce any evidence in this House to support the findings of the grains group. He also spoke of education. I wonder what the cost of documents of this kind is to the taxpayers in order to try and educate the farmer with regard to the metric system. On December 21 the minister spoke in the House in support of this bill. I wish to quote from page 2229 of Hansard, where he stated:
Metric System
Increasing Canada's exports is also one of the key reasons why it makes good economic sense to go metric.
I challenge the minister to prove that the transfer to the metric system in the farming community will add one bushel of wheat to production, or one kernel of grain as far as our exports are concerned. For many years the grain trade has been selling on the export market using the metric system. Therefore, at this time it will not add to our exports.
What does this bill do? Basically, the bill amends the Wheat Board Act, the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act and the Western Grain Stabilization Act by substituting the word "hectares" for "acres" and "tonnes" for "bushels". Yesterday the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) spoke at length on our land titles system, the Torrens system. It is a system that has been effective and efficient over the years. It is one of the best registration systems in the world.
The land titles system is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces and can only be changed by the provincial legislatures. To do so would involve the changing of hundreds of thousands of titles at a cost of hundreds of thousands of dollars. However, if this bill goes through as it is, and undoubtedly it will unless the government accepts some amendments, hectares will be forced upon the farmers in the west, with the result that eventually the western land titles system will have to be changed. What will we then have in Canada? We will have two systems-in effect, a dual system. The Canadian Wheat Board area, namely the prairies, will be using hectares for the measurement of area and the rest of Canada will be using the acreage measurement.
Land in western Canada was surveyed many years ago before it was homesteaded. It was surveyed into mile-square blocks of 640 acres. Then, of course, there is the half-section, the quarter-section and the legal subdivision. These units cannot easily be converted to the metric system. For example, if my mathematics is correct, one section, or 640 acres, will equal 258.8080 hectares.
The farmer in western Canada has used the measurement of acres all his life. He can walk into a field, look at it and say "there are 'X' number of acres in that parcel of land." It is a system with which he is familiar. He can make one pass with a piece of machinery through a field and, knowing the width of the machine, can say that he has cultivated, combined or swathed "X" number of acres. However, if he has to use hectares, what will happen? The powers that be have suggested a simple method. I have here a pamphlet entitled "The Metric System for Farmers". It states:
Probably the best way for you to visualize a hectare, is to put red flags on the fence posts at the four corners of an area measuring one hectare. Each time you look at these flags you will become more familiar with the hectare.
I wonder whether the government is planning to supply red flags to the farmers in western Canada. There is also an effect on the calibration of sprayers used for spraying pesticides and herbicides. The sprayers are all based on acres. Herbicides and pesticides are all packaged in Imperial measure. What will happen when they are sold by the litre instead of by the gallon? The farmer has a choice. He can take a gallon-measur-

January 27, 1977
Metric System
ing can and pour the pesticide or herbicide into the can, thus measuring a gallon, but this is a dangerous practice because in most cases he is dealing with a dangerous poison which must be handled with care. Alternatively, he can make a calculation to convert litres or kilograms into the Imperial system. This is a calculation which involves fractions or decimals and there is a great possibility of error in doing the calculation. If there is a mistake and the chemical is too strong, it will kill the plant. If it is not strong enough, it will be ineffective. An error in calculation could be very costly.
If a farmer buys registered seed, he will be buying it in kilograms. For comparative purposes in measuring the success of his crop from one year to another he will have to convert tonnes per hectare into bushels per acre. What will the bill accomplish in its present form? It will do nothing except cause inconvenience and frustration to farmers. It will add nothing to their efficiency. It will not add one penny to their sales.
I ask hon. members to examine the bill carefully and read some of the material which has been published in connection with it. I quote from a pamphlet entitled "Metric Conversion and the Grain Market" put out by the Canadian Livestock Feed Board and having to do with grain transportation. It reads in part:
The grain transport industry will continue to use the present system for some years yet. No official date has been set for the rail and road transport systems to go metric in freight rate quotations. When the metric system is introduced, the maritime tariffs will be posted in both Imperial and metric terms.
As the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) said a few minutes ago, the elevators will continue to purchase grain in tons and convert in into bushels when it is loaded on to the cars. Subsequently it will be reconverted into metric form at the export end. Since this is the situation, why should it be necessary to move the metric system back into the farmyard? Why not buy from the farmer in bushels and let him continue to use acres? We see here another example of a government of bureaucrats and academics interfering with the producer. I must say that in this case they are aided by the grain companies. Some years ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said the government had no place in the bedrooms of the nation. I say the government has no place in the farmyard. I do not object to metrication beyond the local elevator stage. This makes sense; The grain trade wants it and has been using it for years in connection with export markets. But for heaven's sake leave the producer alone. I might say that it is our intention, when this bill gets to report stage, to put forward amendments which would have the effect of letting the farmer continue to use "acres" and "bushels".
The minister and others on the government side have indicated that there is an urgency attached to this measure and that the bill must be passed by February 1. Presumably, Mr. Speaker, the work which has been done in the grain trade and by the Wheat Board in converting to the metric system has gone on for a considerable time, possibly for some months. Why has the government waited until the eleventh hour before bringing in this legislation? Surely parliament is entitled to
(Mr. Neil.]
have the opportunity and the time to discuss such an important piece of legislation without being under pressure. I like to think that we live under a democratic system in this country, but it seems to me, when I see the government legislating increasingly by way of regulation and bringing in bills at the eleventh hour, the subject matter of which is a fait accompli, that the virtues of our democratic system can no longer be taken for granted.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to register my protest against this type of legislation. We come back to Ottawa and find ourselves called upon to discuss television in the chamber and conversion to the metric system. Surely, with the country facing the desperate problems of which we are all aware, there should be more substantive issues to be debated here.
Bill C-23 makes changes in a number of acts including the Canadian Wheat Board Act, the Gas Inspection Act, the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act, the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, the Regional Development Incentives Act, the Two-Price Wheat Act, the Weights and Measures Act, and the Western Grains Stabilization Act. This is an important bill for grain producers in particular and for agriculture generally. We in western Canada know that "metric day" for the grain industry is February 1, 1977. Yet here we are debating second reading of this bill on January 27, 1977, with just a few days to go. The bill has to be passed before all the arrangements which have been made are legal.
The government knew this long ago. We might well ask why such a long delay has occurred. I do not know where all the other industries are going in this metric conversion process, but I do know that the grain industry is going to get there first. The government has so little respect for agriculture that it has not seen fit to appoint a new deputy minister to the department. We have been without one for two months following the disaster of the last deputy minister.
This is something which must give producers across the country cause to ponder. Where are we in the grain industry going? After the expenditure of hundreds of millions of taxpayers' money on hopper cars, railway trackage and improvements on the west coast, I find that though we used to export 30 million bushels a month from Vancouver, the average so far this year has been 17 million bushels a month-and this is without interference from labour problems or railway problems. With a little more help like metric conversion we shall be right out of business. We find vessels waiting at Vancouver and giving rise to demurrage charges up to $10,000 a day in some cases. All this has to be paid by the western farmer.
We are told by the government that metric conversion is good for us. Well, Mr. Speaker, we do not really need much more of this kind of help from the government. The very disappointing final payment on bread wheat is one small symptom of the malaise in the great grain industry that we used to have. Metric conversion is just another cross for the western producer to bear, another millstone around his neck.
January 27, 1977

As has been said before, our customers have always been able to buy our grain on the basis of metric tonnes, short tons, long tons-any way they wanted. I see no reason to go right back to the producer to change our system. Not only will this change not produce one extra bushel of grain or generate one dollar more of revenue for the producers, but it is going to cost them plenty. It will cost at least $1,000 for every country elevator that we have. We have 3,000; that amounts to $3 million. It will cost each producer at least $100. We have 150,000 of them, so there is another $15 million. Throw in the terminal conversion and you have $20 million right off the bat. That is a lot of money to spend at this time.
Mention has been made of the fact that our land has been surveyed under the Torrens system of miles. We have had a ten-unit system in western Canada for years. We have had telephone poles down every road allowance at steps of ten acres per half-mile. Generations of farmers will be converting back to acres and to bushels because they will see these measurements every time they step on to their land. The people of western Canada are not going to ask for so many litres of gas for their cars; they are going to ask for $5 or $7 worth of gas. They will find their way around this, and I suggest the farmers will do the same thing.
I plead with the government to exempt land measurement from the metric conversion, just as the United States of America will do. It is the same old, familiar story and it is one of the reasons why this government is in so much trouble today. The person required to pay the shot is having less and less of a say as to how his money is being spent. All we hear is that the government knows what is good for us.
I do not see why we cannot have voluntary conversion at the producer level, Mr. Speaker. I can see companies like Massey-Harris, Ford, machine companies and international manufacturers pushing this sort of a deal, but I cannot see why we do not implement it slowly and have voluntary conversion at the producer level.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) has already said that there is a great difference between sitting in a nice, warm office with a calculator, and standing out in a cold, dusty Saskatchewan field trying to calculate chemical conversions. Ounces and acres are well understood in Saskatchewan; it is a tried and true system. One mistake in the calculation of a chemical formula and a farmer's crop could be gone.
I want to go back and refer to some of the information that has been put out and supplied to producers across the country. I have one pamphlet which is headed "Getting Ready for Metric Conversion", and it reads as follows:
How many tonnes of wheat, barley, or oats will your truck hold?
Simple!. .. Suppose you find the truck box is 246 cm by 524 cm, or in metres that's 2.46 m by 5.24 m. Calculate the area of the box floor in square metres by multiplying 2.46 x 5.24 and you will get 12.89 m2.
Now, say you have a level load of wheat that is 1.20 m. (120 cm) deep. How many tonnes are in the box? That depends on how much volume of grain will give one tonne. So you need to know the volume, which is easily found by
Metric System
multiplying the floor area (12.89 m2) by the depth (1.20 m) and you get 15.47 m3.
How many tonnes in 15.47 m3 of wheat? This table will help.
Then a table follows. It goes on to say that using the same table a farmer can calculate the depth of one tonne of grain in his truck box in this way:
-We have a floor area of 12.89 m2 that will be loaded with wheat that has a volume of 1.30 m3 per tonne.
To find the depth of one tonne of wheat, divide its volume by the area of the truck box floor-
In the particular case cited you take 1.30 metres, superscript 2, over 12.89 metres, superscript 2, and you get 0.10 metres, or 10 centimetres. The pamphlet continues.
For a truck box like the one in our illustration, a measuring stick marked at 10 cm intervals will indicate how many tonnes of wheat the truck holds.
I hesitate to repeat this, Mr. Speaker, because it was referred to by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), but it does fascinate me.
You can use a broom-handle or some other straight stick to make a measuring stick for each crop you handle. Remember, each stick is good only for the truck (or bin) for which it is made.

speechtext:
Yes. Then, Mr. Speaker, the pamphlet tells you how to measure your land in metric using the formula of width, times length, in metres, divided by 10,000, giving the area in hectares. The pamphlet continues:
If you don't have the measurements in metres, you can make a conversion using one yard equals 0.91 metre. If you have your land area in acres, multiply the acreage by 0.405 to get the area in hectares. As a rule of thumb, there are 2.5 acres in a hectare.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, where are we going on this thing? This pamphlet is but one of a flood of pamphlets, letters and brochures that have been distributed in western Canada. I have been in almost every country which is a major buyer of Canadian grain. I was chairman of the Board of Grain Commissioners for several years and one of my responsibilities was to help promote Canadian grains in world markets. During my term of office we set many records for exports which have not been surpassed to this day. I have also been a farmer; I have raised many fields of grain in my lifetime. I have been to university and I have been to the odd goat-roping contest; but I can tell hon. members that I do not know what these formulas mean, and they certainly will not mean much to the farmers of western Canada. If it is such a big deal for everyone to convert to the metric system, just think how much more important it would be if we all spoke the same language.
Mention has been made of the railways. Mr. Jim Wright, who is secretary of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, is reported in a Free Press report on farming, dated December 22 last, as saying:
Mr. Wright also expressed concern about the fact the railways don't go metric until 1981. "Right off the bat we'll have a problem because we'll be talking metric and they'll be talking pounds.''

Metric System
He said attempts to have the railways bill elevators for the movement of grain on a per tonne or per kilogram basis have failed, because much of their rail traffic is non-grain and has not yet converted to metric.
The Regina Leader-Post carried an article on this subject, part of which is as follows:
Strong objections to the metric conversion program came from Larry Brown, executive secretary of the Saskatchewan Federation of Labour.
Mr. Brown said metric conversion's main purpose is to facilitate trade between large multinational corporations and will have little impact on individual Canadians.
"If there is any benefit at all to individual working Canadians, it's extremely remote," he said.
While some unionized workers have contracts requiring their employers to pay all or part of the cost of new, metric tools, he said many workers have no such agreements or are outside unions. Many workers will have to keep dual sets of metric and Imperial tools until vehicles and construction supplies in Imperial dimensions have disappeared, he added.
All one need do, Mr. Speaker, is think of the number of dual inventories which will have to be kept across this country to get some idea of the cost of metric conversion to this nation. In conclusion, I would ask the government to give us in western Canada a break. Would the government at least give us some assurance that our land will be exempt from metric conversion, that there will be no change to our land tenure system? Earlier today the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, did not give that assurance. I hope we will get that assurance from the government.

speechtext:
I do not want to take a lot of time in closing the debate on second reading. I have listened to many concerns expressed by members on the other side and I know that the farmers of this country have some apprehension about this change that will be taking place. Change very often does cause difficulty. I recall the change from Fahrenheit to Celsius when all kinds of concerns were expressed by the general population. It is my hope that during the committee hearings we will be able to explain and deal with many of the points that have been raised by hon. members.
It is my belief that some pretty good explanations can be given about the suggested changes and the planning that has taken place and, hopefully, we can go ahead with this legislation in the spirit with which the metric commission has proceeded and in which the various sector groups have operated. In fact, the sector committee on agriculture has been

working on this for a few years. That committee has been heavily involved in planning for those changes being implemented that will affect the farmers.
I know that some at the farming level suggested that appropriate consultation has not taken place. If hon. members are telling me this, I believe them; but that certainly was not the intent. A great deal of information has been sent out to farmers and their organizations have been consulted. We have widely canvassed farm organizations throughout the country, including the National Farmers Union, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and others. For example, the grain elevator companies are definitely in favour of this legislation. They are anxious to have it implemented by February 1 so that at least this part of the metric conversion program can go ahead. As a matter of fact, they are all geared up and ready to move.
Because of the nature and quantity of planning that has taken place involving the general farming public, hopefully this change can take place with a minimum of difficulty and with a minimum of partisanship. It is certainly not our intention to move ahead in any partisan way. Hopefully, in committee we can explain how the changes will take place. We will adopt a flexible attitude, and perhaps after some explanation regarding the difficulties involved we will be able to arrive at solutions. We have looked at some of the experiences of other countries.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext: Are you going to preserve the acre?

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext:
We will have a look at that and discuss it very thoroughly. We have already asked some experts of the metric commission and of the grain trade to be ready to give the explanations necessary and outline some of the difficulties involved in mixing the system, such as using acres and tonnes or tonnes and bushels. We would like to avoid confusion as much as possible. But by mixing the system we are bound to introduce some degree of confusion. For instance, if we are going to have tonnes and acres there is bound to be confusion.
I am told that other countries, for instance Australia, have gone cold turkey all the way. They have gone full metric and have experienced less difficulty in the implementation of their program over the long-term, as opposed to the United Kingdom where there has been a bit of a mixed system. They tried to maintain some of the Imperial system terminology and have had difficulty. The change has not been as successful as it might have been. The conclusion we have come to in looking at the experience of other countries is that we should avoid mixing the system, and I hope this can be explained fully by the experts in the committee.
Several of my friends across the way have suggested that we are not going to sell more grain as a result of conversion. I admit that fact and realize that grain has been selling throughout the world on a metric system for years. We admit that this will not sell more grain. The selling of grain around the world does not depend on metric conversion; it depends on markets, whether Russia and China have good or bad crops.
If hon. members look a little closer at the statements I have made they will see I have suggested there are opportunities in

other areas if we go metric. I am told, for instance, that in the lumber trade there are opportunities in the European markets if we are able to make more materials available in metric measurement. There are opportunities in other areas as well.
It has been said many times that we are one of the last countries in the world to go metric. The United States is also going metric and is well on the way. We hope we can remain a step ahead of the United States in the change so that we will be ahead in at least our metric conversion program. We have very close liaison with the United States on metric conversion. They have been in touch with our people, particularly those in the grain trade. We still hope we can take the lead in this regard, but the United States will not be far behind in converting.
I have some rather extensive notes dealing with a number of points that have been made, but rather than try to deal with them all during this debate I will leave them until we have an opportunity to answer in committee. Hopefully, the committee stage will not be prolonged. It is hoped that its deliberations will be shortened by having experts in attendance who can answer questions to the satisfaction of the farmers and others.
