speechtext:
It being five o'clock, it is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the House that the questions to be raised at the time of adjournment are as follows: The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cros-bie)-Fisheries-Proposed plan for compensation for fishermen engaged in redfish fishery-Request for report; the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes)-Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-Objection to documentary on French culture in village of Paincourt; the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek)-External Affairs- Reason for alleged secret expulsion from Canada of Mr. Perdomo, representative of Cuba.
Bell Canada
It being five o'clock, this House will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely, private bills, notices of motions and public bills.

that Bill S-2, an act respecting Bell Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
He said: Mr. Speaker, before reviewing the highlights of Bill S-2 relating to Bell Canada I would like to provide some brief background information on the company and the bill. In addition, Mr. Speaker, because a private bill such as this must of necessity be sponsored by a private member, I should perhaps state that I have not been, and am not now, a shareholder of Bell Canada or its affiliates and have no pecuniary interest in the bill before us.
Bell Canada was incorporated in 1880 by a special act of parliament which has since been amended 12 times to increase its authorized share capital and to update its charter. The last time the company applied to parliament for amendments to its act of incorporation was in 1968 when it was authorized, among other things, to increase its capital and to issue preferred stock. The company's intention to proceed with these proposed amendments was widely advertised in various newspapers and government official gazettes during four consecutive weeks last fall, following which the bill was introduced in the other place and received third reading on December 15, 1976.
As to the bill itself, it has four main purposes: first, to increase the maximum authorized share capital of the company; second, to modernize the financing provisions of its charter; third, to update the corporate powers; and fourth, to enable the company to alter its objects, powers and share capital by letters patent subject, however, to cancellation by a negative resolution in either house of parliament.
Bell Canada requests authorization to increase its share capital to $5 billion from the present limit of $1.75 billion. Since 1945 increased share capital authorizations have been applied for and granted by parliament about every decade. The increase of $3.25 billion now being sought by the company is prompted by the need to finance part of the huge capital programs required to provide the services expected by the public. The company's business is highly capital-intensive and requires the investment of massive amounts of money which are provided by internally-generated funds on the one hand and by debt and equity financing on the other hand. The company forecasts capital expenditures of $15 billion over the

Bell Canada
next decade. It anticipates that it will exhaust its current limit of $1.75 billion of share capital by the end of 1978.
In order to obtain large sums from the capital markets to meet increasing demands for telecommunication services, Bell Canada must compete both at home and abroad with other firms and governments which enjoy a much greater financial flexibility. For example, under its present charter Bell Canada cannot issue shares other than common shares of $25 par value and preferred shares, nor can it split its shares or consolidate them. It cannot borrow under the authority of a general borrowing by-law. Accordingly, a certain number of proposed amendments are designed to equip the company with similar financing flexibility to that enjoyed by practically every company nowadays. May I point out also that most of these financing amendments are similar or identical to the provisions of Bill S-ll, an act respecting British Columbia Telephone Company adopted by parliament in December, 1974.
Included in these financing amendments is a provision enabling the company to issue its share capital in the future without CRTC approval, although within the $5 billion limit set out in this bill. Since 1929 the company has been required under its charter to obtain the approval of the regulatory body, formerly the Canadian Transport Commission, with respect to the amount, terms and conditions of each stock issue. This requirement was understandable and relevant in the circumstances down to the year 1966 when its relevancy disappeared.
The purpose of the CRTC approval of share issues was to ensure that the company would not sell new stock at a price, for example at a low price, which would impose undue costs on its customers. This was during the time when the company's earnings and rates were regulated on the basis of the total number of shares outstanding. Since May, 1966, however, the formula adopted by the regulatory body for regulating earnings and rates has completely changed. The company's permitted earnings are now stated as a percentage of the total amount of capital invested in the business and not at all related to the number of shares outstanding. The result is that the continuing requirement for CRTC approval of share issues is now redundant. This matter will, as in the past, be dealt with by the ceiling provided from time to time and by authorization received from the company's shareholders.
At this point I should like to emphasize that repeal of this requirement would leave absolutely intact the CRTC's jurisdiction over the company's rates for services offered to the public. All of that essential regulatory process would remain intact. But this single change of eliminating approval of specific stock issues would do more than terminate a practice that has lost its relevancy because of the new rate-regulating formula. It would also preclude delays associated with public hearings, thereby assuring more flexibility in the timing of a stock issue, often important for advantageous pricing in the market and for staying within the short time limits provided for in underwriting agreements. This gain in flexibility is important as the competition for equity capital becomes more intense.
The third aim of the bill is to modernize the corporate powers of the company through the incorporation into its charter of section 16 of the Canada Corporations Act. The amendment proposed to achieve this objective would clarify and broaden the existing ancillary and incidental powers of the company. It would allow the company to invest in other companies having objects in whole or in part similar to those of Bell Canada. It would enable Bell Canada to implement government policy regarding the provisions of computer services by communication carriers through separate arm's length affiliates.
The application of section 16 of the company would, in effect, place it on the same level as most other companies which can carry out their objects in the most appropriate manner without being hampered by the constraints which presently preclude Bell Canada, except in very limited cases, from incorporating or acquiring subsidiaries to perform activities it could undertake itself.
O)
The powers sought here would only be exercisable as incidental and ancillary to the objects set out in the company's charter. These powers were, in essence, made applicable to Telesat Canada, a federally-regulated telecommunications carrier.
Finally, the last purpose of the bill is to authorize the company to alter its objects, powers and share capital in the future by applying to the minister of consumer and corporate affairs who is the registrar general for letters patent, which would however be subject to being nullified by either House of parliament during a period of 30 sitting days following their tabling in parliament. This is the negative resolution procedure which is found in one form in the Telesat Canada Act and in a modified and detailed version recently provided in the Income Tax Conventions Act, 1976. The proposed change would not deprive parliament of its control over the company's charter but, rather, would modify the manner in which such control would continue to be exercised.
Mr. Speaker, these are the highlights of Bill S-2. Hon. members will appreciate that full opportunity will be given to examine the bill in detail when it is dealt with in committee, where the company's chief officers will make themselves available as witnesses. These proposed amendments update the capital and the powers of Bell Canada. They provide it with the financing and corporate flexibility required in the field of telecommunications today and for the future. They leave intact the essential regulatory role of the CRTC while equipping the company to meet the service needs of Canadians in the period ahead.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to recommend these amendments to the consideration of hon. members.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) on Bill S-2 which had its birth in the other place. I know others will be participating in

January 27, 1977

this debate and might make some irrelevant comments about the birth of such a bill in the other place, and will undoubtedly colour the air with purple prose on the relationship of such bills and corporate legislation starting in the other place. But I do not intend to make prolonged remarks at this stage on the stand of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition on Bill S-2 because, basically, as the hon. member for Scarborough East said, the motion is to refer this bill to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications which will give a better opportunity for us to make a more exhausive study of certain aspects of this complicated bill.
Having been in this chamber for a few years, I know that every time "Mother Bell" is mentioned there is no doubt this gives an opportunity to any politican to wax eloquent and often irresponsible about that Canadian company. Like the hon. member for Scarborough East, I speak as one of those commoners in the land who does not have a pecuniary interest in the company other than to pay my telephone bill in Ontario, because another telephone company sends me its bills in Atlantic Canada.
I think the Bell Telephone Company is a perfect example of a schizophrenic personality, which is often that of a Canadian politician. It is both remarkable and paradoxical that often those who champion and espouse the so-called nationalism and proclaim all the great sentiments and strong views about being Canadian and about freedom from coast to coast-and, incidentally, having a good telephone service from coast to coast- are the very people, and we may hear from some in this chamber, who as soon as "Mother Bell" is mentioned will say that she is an unhealthy or tainted woman with a tainted heritage and that she is wearing soiled clothes.
Without getting into a provocative debate on this issue with the hon. member for Scarborough East, let me say that Bill S-2 has four main aims, as the hon. member said.
I must confess that I cannot give a full and detailed explanation of the first one in terms of what the corporate wizards could do with some of the changes to the capital procedure, but I know that unless parliament moves on Bell Telephone's request for increased capital authorization, hon. members will be asking in this chamber why certain communities were not hooked up to the telephone service and why this company does not provide the service that we expect from it. The request by the company to increase its authorized capital from $1.75 billion to $5 billion involves the international workings of the company and its construction program for the next ten years.
Any hon. member here would be handicapped in trying to justify such a fundamentally large construction program, and the only people who can do that are the officers of the company who will appear before the committee. I will not get into a debate with the hon. member for Scarborough East on this subject, but I did ask, as a matter of historical interest, about the history of charter amendments of the company and I find myself with somewhat different information from that given to us by the hon. member for Scarborough East. I thought there were only ten changes. For the record, I will spell out the ten changes in the charter of the company which
Bell Canada
perhaps show the rate of inflation in this country as well as the development of the Bell Telephone Company from its origin as an innovater and leader way back at its inception. It also shows what has happened with the value of money and the size of the company today.
The first authorization for an increase in capital was in 1880, and it was for $1 million. In 1884 it went up to $2 million. In 1892 we moved ahead to $5 million, and in 1902 to $10 million. In 1906 we went up to $30 million, and in 1920- a longer gap than the decade mentioned by the hon. member- we went up to $75 million. In 1929 we went up to $150 million. Then there was a long gap when we had a depression and a war. In 1948 the next change in the charter to increase the capital was for $500 million. In 1957 we went up to $1 billion, and the last change that has been mentioned was in 1968, to $1.75 billion. Now the proposed change is to $5 billion.
I am advised by officers of the Bell Company that while this is a pretty healthy leap forward in terms of the corporate authorization, in terms of continuing and expanding the service, it will just provide the basis for the capital works program in the next ten years. I should like to hear the responsible officers come before the committee with research on some of the intricate provisions, so that we may be able to ask sensible questions of them and hear their reasons for the increase from $1.75 billion to $5 billion.
I do not find any real objection to modernizing the financial provisions of the act by putting the company in the same position as the B.C. Telephone Company and incorporating similar provisions to those in the Canada Corporations Act. Some reason that this bill would put Bell into the same position as other companies in terms of competing for funds in the money markets so that it could compete and not be penalized when getting equity capital and thereby it would not have to charge that much, hopefully, to its subscribers. I agree with that argument to a point, but without getting into all the statistics of the uniqueness of Bell Telephone, it is clear that Bell is not like all the other companies. Perhaps that is one of the reasons we have this archaic procedure-and there is no disrespect intended to the hon. member for Scarborough East. However, the only way the federal charter can be changed is for it to come through these halls under a private member's bill and to have it sponsored here.
Nationalize it.

Having been in some countries which have nationalized their telephone systems, and in at least two provinces of this country where the telephone systems are nationalized, and having used those telephone systems, I have no faith at all in government-run telephone systems providing better service to the average person-
What about Alberta?

-than the service we get from Bell.

January 27, 1977
Bell Canada
It is much better.

The hon. member will have a chance to speak in the debate. I am referring to the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) who is from the nationalized state of Saskatchewan. It does not really matter what part you are from, once you leave the cities, because it is pretty well blended into the socialistic porridge pot-and porridge is pretty bland. However, there is not a person who has travelled around the world and who has used the telephone systems in other parts of the world who can show me a telephone system better than the Bell Telephone system.
Hear, hear!
By saying that, I do not claim to be an apologist for Bell.
What about the one in Russia?

We do not have to go to Russia: we can go to France, Great Britain or Saskatchewan. Some hon. members could go further than that where there are no telephones, because they do not need telephones to be heard.
Oh, oh!
Be that as it may, this is basically a corporate bill.
Oh, oh!

My hon. friends are already starting to attack the walls of capitalism. It is interesting to note the schizophrenic character of this country and of hon. members who think they have a monopoly on ideology. I can mention parts of this bill which give me a great deal of concern, but in terms of my trying to talk in a knowledgeable way about whether at this stage authorizing an increase in authorized capital from $1.75 billion to $5 billion I do not know if I or my friends can make knowledgeable comments.
This bill was debated in the other place by senators. I know hon. members to my left do not have a senator there, and if the House leader of the New Democratic Party, the shadow leader-not the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), but his seatmate-had his way, of course there would not be a Senate. However, even in that chamber of sober second thought many thought that Bell Telephone was controlled by I.T. and T. Evidently they forgot the fact that Bell Telephone is owned 98 per cent by John Q. Canadian, or Mr. Canadian. However, I will not go too far with that.
With regard to modernizing the financial provisions, I will be interested at the committee stage to see just what the officers say about these things. If changes can be made to keep Bell in a competitive position in financial markets by seeking equity capital without penalty to its subscribers, including the widows and orphans of this land who sometimes use the telephone, then I will be in favour of that; but I think we have to listen to the argument that under the Canada Corporations Act all companies are supposed to be put into a similar

position. Obviously, Bell Canada is not a company like others, and that is both its curse and its challenge. It is a curse to those who want to curse a very efficient company which provides us with good service, yet it is a challenge to Bell's developing further. There is a little conflict here and I will be interested to see how the evidence comes out.
As the hon. member says, the reason we can have this change now is that the rate of return is on a different base, and because it is on a different base-which was, I think, set in 1966, which was the effective time change for the rate not being based on the return of issued shares but on equity capital and investment capital-you do not have to be quite as careful in giving a very large potential increase in the authorized capital permissible under the act.
I am more concerned about the last two purposes of the bill, the changes in the ancillary powers of the company and also the method provided to change the charter in the future. Very quickly, this question of allowing the company to broaden its powers-and, again, using the Canada Corporations Act as the base to give the powers, as is the case with other companies-I think has to be watched fairly carefully. We are in an uncharted world as a result of changing technology, and today we are asked to incorporate section 16 of the Canada Corporations Act which would allow the company to invest in other companies having objects altogether, or in part, similar to those of this company. That is, in effect, the purpose of these changes. Yet we have had, and will continue to have, in this House questions, answers and debates as to the literal interpretation of "broadcasting." The Broadcasting Act was passed in 1966, and the word "cable" does not even appear in it.
We have here a communications company, Bell, which missed a golden opportunity when it did not get into cable years ago when telephone companies had the first crack at it. Other telephone companies as well would not touch cable with a ten-foot pole. Hon. members to my left would not touch it even with a ten-foot telephone pole. Hon. members to my left would not appreciate this, but it was small entrepreneurs who took the chance and the risk, and that has made Canada the leader in the world with regard to cable.
I know at the moment there are socialist governments in certain parts of the country who would like to reverse this clock and get provincial telephone companies directly into the cable field. I am prepared to say, with no fundamental disrespect-other than that I think it is wrong-that if the provincial telephone companies get into those areas they will not be able to provide the service that subscribers are getting from small cable companies. At the moment some areas do not even have cable service because of this jurisdictional fight.
I feel that there is one area which has to be watched cautiously. Using the argument that these changes will put Bell into the same position as other companies-and I am prepared to admit that Bell is not the same as other companies-I think parliament has a duty, and when we get into committee we should examine the officers of the company as to the full implications of these ancillary powers with special reference to Bell as a telephone company which obviously has
January 27, 1977

an interest in the computer field and now would perhaps like to develop an interest in the cable area.
Not an interest, a monopoly.

You have monopolies in Manitoba and Saskatchewan with your phone companies. The section which gives me the greatest concern-and, as outlined in the bill, would not get my support-is the section the hon. member for Scarborough East mentioned. I refer to the procedural clause which in effect sets up a negative resolution whereby the company could hereafter change its objects, let alone its purposes. So far as I am concerned, we ought to look with a negatively critical eye at that clause requiring the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) to bring before this House for a certain period of scrutiny the letters patent.
Let me hasten to add that Bell is not like other companies. It provides good service, and needs funds to continue that service. I know that the company wants immediately a more expeditious way for changing its charter. It wants to be more businesslike in providing good service for the Canadian people. Yet Bell is not like other companies, and is not analagous to Telesat. It may be intended to follow the Telesat precedent. However, Telesat is unique, and Telesat really is not part of the commercial world. That satellite is in orbit in the heavens, providing channels of communication on a commercial basis to large organizations, including the CBC.
And Bell.

And Bell. Really, I am concerned about the negative provision of the bill. Bell as a company is intimately involved with consumers in Ontario and Quebec. I question the wisdom of the negative provision of the bill; after all, the company is involved in the field of communications and we do not know what fundamental changes may come about even three years down the road.
In 1968, when I participated in debate on the Broadcasting Act, the House was not thinking of the effect of satellites, communication by satellite, and the computer technology which has burst forth on the horizon. Yet we all know that this new technology is fundamentally important now to the communications industry, but it has also created some new problems. Therefore by giving the company certain powers by way of a negative resolution you would enable it to change its charter, let alone the purposes of its creation. If you go that far, any pretense of parliamentary direction and/or control will go out of the window. But that is a procedural point which does not go to the principle of the matter, namely, that Bell needs money in order to continue good service. The company may be somewhat extravagant, to my way of thinking-
Extravagant?
-extravagant in asking for unrestricted ancillary powers which, obviously, would make Bell bigger.

Who needs it?
Bell Canada
The hon. member's party in Manitoba-

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak too long, because I know my friend to my left is chafing at the bit. The party to my left cannot wait to add its constructive thoughts to what has already been said. I will not impose on the good graces of hon. members who have allowed me extra time, because I know that we want to hear other points of view on this bill.
I see no fundamental objection to the request concerning authorized capital. After all that goes to the root of our present debate. I think the provision regarding ancillary powers must be looked at with a critical eye. Certainly the negative resolution provision as presently contained in the Bill S-2 ought to be revised. I am aware of the company's interest in a procedure which will allow it to make certain changes expeditiously. However, as a parliamentarian not involved with the company, I want to see the maintenance of parliamentary direction and control. If the negative resolution provision presently contained in the bill is allowed to remain, you may as well kiss such parliamentary control goodbye.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make some remarks on Bill S-2 concerning the financing powers of Bell Canada.
The previous speaker tried to leave the impression that Bell is mainly concerned about modernizing and changing some of the legislation which affects the way Bell raises its capital. I submit that is not the essential point of this bill. In essence, we are determining to what degree we shall still be able to maintain effective regulation over Bell Canada as it changes its capacity to raise funds. That, it seems to me, is the crux of the matter about which hon. members ought to be cautious before rushing ahead and changing existing legislation.
Bill S-2 has three main aims; I will enumerate them, in order to elaborate my concerns about the contents of the bill. First, the bill would allow Bell to borrow, issue stock, bonds, debentures and other securities as the company itself deems necessary, but without the approval of the regulatory agency, the CRTC.

Shame!

Bell Canada

Second, the bill would broaden the company's powers by revoking its present act of incorporation and placing Bell under the provisions of the Canada Corporations Act.
Third, the bill would allow Bell to charge the going rate of interest on overdue customer accounts, instead of the current rate of 6 per cent allowed by the CRTC.
What will be the effect if Bill S-2 passes? In my opinion Bill S-2 is an attempt by Bell to undermine the public regulation of that monopoly. In effect it would put Bell's corporate interest above that of its customers. Because Bell is a telecommunications monopoly, the only protection its subscribers have at this point is government regulation. I submit that the public regulation of Bell must not be lessened or weakened. How then would Bill S-2 weaken the public regulation of Bell Canada?
Let me deal with the first point I mentioned, the changes in Bell's method of capitalization. To see this in its proper context we should look at the history of the rate regulation of Bell. In 1919 the government regulated the earnings per share; this continued until 1966. That regulation was designed to protect the public by preventing Bell from making excessive profits per share. However, over the years Bell deliberately circumvented this means of regulation by watering the stock, that is to say, selling stock to existing shareholders at prices well below the market value and passing on monopoly profits in the form of capital gains rather than income. We find that in 1929 parliament revised the Bell act, to require regulatory approval for all issues of stock. In 1966 Bell succeeded in getting a revision of regulations, replacing control on earnings per share with percentage return on average total capital.
I submit that through this bill Bell wants to remove all regulation of what stocks Bell issues and at what price. What is the danger in this change? It is this. If the government is serious about regulating Bell in the public interest, it must regulate two things. It must regulate earnings per share and the issue price of equity, and not just the percentage return on capital, as is the present case.
If Bill S-2 passes, the CRTC will have no power to authorize the terms and conditions of new stock issues, that is to say, it will be unable to regulate Bell Canada effectively. I will give an example of how this will come about. What will happen is that Bell will issue preferred shares, with very large dividends. It will then be able to argue that common share dividends must exceed those of preferred shares or else investors will not convert their shares. The way that Bell will get common shares up in value will be to argue before the CRTC that it needs to increase subscribers' telephone rates. The NDP, therefore, in the interest of telephone subscribers must oppose this attempt by Bell to escape regulation.
The second change that the bill proposes is to change the act of incorporation under which Bell now lives. The present act states that, first, Bell Canada is to engage only in the provision of telecommunications service. Second, Bell is to act solely as a common carrier. Third, Bell is to own as subsidiaries only

companies engaged in telegraphic or telephonic communications.
What Bill S-2 wants to do is replace the above provisions under Bell's act of incorporation with the Canada Corporations Act. This would enable Bell to participate in any or all markets it wished to. In other words, Bell claims it should be treated as any other corporation.
Bell Canada by no flight of the imagination can be considered just like any other corporation. It is a monopoly, and a very powerful one at that. Ninety-three per cent of its revenue is based on telephone service. Only 7 per cent comes from competitive operations such as data services. It certainly cannot be considered like any other corporation in the private sector.
What are the implications of Bell coming under the provisions of the Canada Corporations Act? Bell could expand its operations and earning ability in areas which would be beyond present CRTC regulation. Bell could go before the CRTC and plead poverty on its telephone operations and thereby get a rate increase, when in fact it is making large profits from other investments which would not be taken into account by the CRTC. There is already ample evidence of this occurring within the present framework of operations of Bell Canada. I will give the example of Northern Electric.
In the past the Canadian Transport Commission, which used to regulate Bell, was very negligent in failing to take into account Bell's relationship with Northern Electric and its other subsidiaries when trying to assess Bell's profitability. For example, in 1974 Bell's share of net income from Northern Electric was in excess of $48 million, but the profitability of Bell's subsidiaries is never examined when Bell comes before the regulatory agency pleading for a rate increase.
It is my contention that the CRTC, which is now charged with examining Bell's rate increases, should be looking at its relationship with its subsidiaries, as well as at the other fact that has been neglected to date. That is the fact that Bell has been able to defer paying over $650 million taxes through a deferred tax scheme. This is no longer counted as a liability by accountants. In reality what Bell has here is an interest free loan that has never been taken into account when the government assesses Bell's profitability.
Looking at Bell's profit over the past few years, I submit it has been more than adequate. In 1975, for example, Bell's profit was $266,784,000, an increase of 18.9 per cent over
1974.	For the first nine months of 1976 its profit was $218,415,000 compared to $187,746,000 for the first nine months of
1975,	an increase of approximately 16 per cent.
And that in a period of controls.

As my colleague from Nickel Belt says, that was in a period of controls. Since Bell is a monopoly it cannot be treated as any other corporation. Therefore it must not come under the purview of the Canada Corporations Act.
The third thing Bill S-2 tries to do, as I mentioned, is change the charge on overdue accounts which is currently
January 27, 1977

limited at 6 per cent. Bell wants to raise it to the going rate, which I presume is somewhere around 11 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, I apologize for interrupting, but I am sure the hon. member, by misunderstanding the clause, does not want to mislead us. It is not overdue customer accounts. It is the overdue accounts for shares of those who are subscribing to new shares.

I thank the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) for that correction. I would not have much difficulty in hearing arguments along this line being put forward by Bell. This is one of the least distasteful parts of the bill. However, I would hope that we could have some kind of commitment from Bell for improvement of service.
In northern Ontario, for example, a situation has existed in the small communities with multiple party lines, where there are as many as ten or more people on one line. I think of people in rural areas who want telephones brought to their homes. In northern Ontario there is an example of one family being charged in excess of $1,000 a year. I might mention also the practice of requiring a $200 deposit from subscribers with overdue accounts. We might look at some of these practices in terms of a trade-off commitment from Bell before any increase in the company's power is permitted by way of a change in the infrastructure.
When I look at the history of Bell and the attempts made by government to regulate it, I find a history of efforts to evade or reduce public regulation of the company. This powerful monopoly has, I submit, been aided and abetted by its friends in the Senate who gave the bill before us only a cursory glance. Bill S-2, if allowed to pass in its present form would, I maintain, subvert the already weak regulatory authority upon which we as consumers have to rely when it comes to keeping this giant corporation in line. In the interest of good telephone service at affordable rates, I submit that the New Democratic Party cannot support a measure which would mean less public control over this powerful monopoly. We need more accountability from Bell, not less.

Mr. Speaker, it may be a little late and I do not want to kill this bill, but I want to say a few words about Bill S-2. It is very unusual to have a bill coming from the Senate. I am always surprised to see something coming out of the other place. I always wonder whether the senators do that for the sake of private or public interest. Anyway, I do not want to criticize the work of our good old senators, but I should only say, Mr. Speaker, that when we read Bell Canada's representations in this bill, they are asking that their charter be amended to be able to increase the capital stock from $3.25 billion to $5 billion.
In my opinion, this is a very considerable increase compared to the increases requested in previous years. I wonder whether Bell Canada wants to go into the electronic or other fields.
Bell Canada
This is a very important request and it deserves serious consideration by the government.
In the explanatory notes we can read this, and I quote:
This amendment would extend and update the borrowing powers of the Company.
Again, this is a request by the company which will enable them to expand very considerably their operations. If we knew the objectives of the telephone company in the most minute detail, and if the sole purpose were to improve telephone service, I would be very happy about it. But, as it is outlined further on, Bell Canada can invest in other companies. That is where the risk lies. It is quite easy for it to invest in other companies in an attempt to create a monopoly against which the government could not exert influence.
So far the government has been quite successful in supervising Bell Canada's operations. I am not prepared to admit that it has to be nationalized; on the contrary, I am against any nationalization. But I just want the House to realize that there are obviously place for improvement in the field of telephone lines. We like to say that we have a good telephone system, that Bell Canada is a good company, a good servant of the population. We must recognize also that it is well taken care of by the government. We must admit, when we see all the favours it obtains from the government, that it would be worthwhile to turn to the consumer and try giving him a little bit more satisfaction. I should like to deal briefly with rural services. I wonder if the House is aware of the fact that there still are rural areas where nine, ten or even twelve parties share the same line. One could understand that thirty years ago but today, with all the credits given the company, I feel it should make an effort to give better service.
I have had occasion to write repeatedly to their office begging them to give private lines, at least to merchants. It is hard to believe that a merchant should have had to share a party line with ten other subscribers, after waiting for a private line for three years. There is a limit to everything.
Mr. Speaker, I would not want that money ...

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
speechtext:
I thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, and I thank hon. members. I wanted to take this opportunity to comment on a matter of interest probably to members in all four corners of this House during this particular debate having regard to the changes proposed to the customs tariff in respect of pork and pork products.
Since the budget of May 25 last, there has been a substantial alteration in the position of pork markets in Canada, and far from being in a position now in which further cuts in the tariff would be required from the consumer standpoint there has, indeed, been a dramatic drop in the cost of pork and pork products. In the circumstances it would appear that in all fairness to pork producers, as I indicated in my second reading speech, it would be appropriate to take action for the purpose of removing the tariff reduction proposed by the bill.
There are two possible ways of doing this; first, with an amended notice of ways and means, and to amend the bill itself in the committee of the whole. The rather more simple way is to follow the procedure suggested in the bill itself, that is, to make provision for an order restoring the level of protection. Under the circumstances, the latter would appear to be the more appropriate. I would now indicate to the House in closing the debate that it would be my intention, as soon as the bill is passed, to seek from the Governor in Council the authority to restore the tariff level on pork in light of the change in the markets.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) wishes to ask a question of the minister, which can only be done with the consent of the minister and the House.
Agreed.

By way of explanation would the minister indicate if this procedure is contemplated in respect of pork products alone, or is this a device he plans on utilizing in respect of textiles and shoes, for example, as a quick means of action without reference to the House by a ways and means motion?

Mr. Speaker, the answer would be no. As I indicated in introducing the bill, the dropping of the protection was available under the act primarily with regard to food commodities, bearing in mind the rather mercurial nature of the food market. Of course this has been more than amply proven by the pork situation so a procedure was included in the bill, and is included in the appropriate clause to restore the protection. My intention would be to apply this with regard to pork only. As the hon. member knows, there are other commodities which are very much the subject of concern
January 27, 1977

and consideration on the part of the government, such as textiles and shoes. My view is that they would not be dealt with by way of a temporary tariff change withdrawal of this kind, but would require more fundamental measures which, of course, would be dealt with under other aspects of our law.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order to ask the minister a brief question, if I may.
How about the committee of the whole? That is what it is for.
We are going into the committee of the whole now?
Yes.
