speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The House in committee of the whole on Bill C-15, to amend the customs tariff.
On Clause 1-Schedule A amended.

Mr. Chairman, this is a very specific clause, I grant you, but there is one point that bothers me a little bit. Notwithstanding some very extensive remarks by members in the House generally, during which questions of principle were raised, the minister has not replied to those points in closing this debate. Unless I raise the matter at this point on Clause 1 we are not going to get the answers. I have specific reference to the point I made as reported in Hansard of Tuesday, October 26, during the second reading debate, as follows:
The minister has not spoken to us about what the government has foreseen with regard to the trade development pattern, not as of yesterday but in the three or four years during which we saw inflation rise at a gallop. I
I know that several of my colleagues have expressed some concern, and it may be that the hon. member for York-Simcoe will have a lot more to say about the nature of negotiations going on in Geneva at the present time under GATT.
There are a number of things that have worried hon. members and these have been expressed in other debates, and we have yet to receive adequate answers. Before we are prepared to discuss the detail under Clause 1 of this bill regarding items changed in Schedule A, I hope the minister will at least give us some indication of the answers he intends to provide, when he will provide them, and whether the government is prepared to allow some government time for a debate on international trade. I am quite serious when I suggest this must be done at this time. The budget debate of last June did not offer an opportunity. The minister in his presentation did not deal sufficiently with the nature of our international trade.
Customs Tariff
We have had some very worrisome deficits in the commodity account, and the whole financial picture in the country is predicated upon a changing pattern of international trade. As I said, I will come back to that later. I know there are some provincial governments which have expressed serious reservations about the nature and composition of the negotiations going on in Geneva. Provincial governments are not having any input whatsoever and items are being traded away, as they were under the Kennedy Round, at an accelerated rate, cutting across the industrial policies of particular provinces. I know the cattle industry was hurt badly, for example, at that time, and it is conceivable that it might be hurt again on this occasion.
I know that various provincial governments have industrial policies for the development of their resources, yet it seems that our negotiators do not even consult the provincial authorities in respect of what might be the best possible stance for Canada. To that extent I would hope the minister will tell us the government's intention regarding these consultations on trade.
There are many other points I raised in my speech. I hope the hon. member for York-Simcoe will elaborate on these particular points.

Mr. Chairman, I would just remind the hon. gentleman that, indeed, we did debate in the House last fall the matter of the government's trade stance. In particular, we had an extensive presentation by a number of responsible members on this side of the House regarding the over-all tariff negotiations.
The hon. member has raised the suggestion that perhaps it would be appropriate to have a second such debate, several months having passed, with a new United States administration having been established. I am certainly prepared to consider that and, of course, to discuss with my colleague, the House leader, the question of additional time. It may well be that, negotiations under the Tokyo round having been at something of a standstill during the election in the United States and when they were active with the change of administration, it is apropos at this time. It seems to me we have here a specific set of tariff changes, specifically directed at the consumer sector, and primarily the food sector, for the purpose of meeting inflation problems in Canada. I wonder whether this bill is the best place for widespread debate on the over-all question of trade policy.
I would like to suggest, in light of the interest that some members have in trying to provide relief for pork producers, that it would be appropriate to pass this bill. The Leader of the Opposition has raised the question of when the next budget will be introduced. It seems to me we should not be introducing a new budget until we dispose of the bills arising from the May 25 budget. I would hope we might have some debate directed to the specific items in this bill and I would hope for a broad debate on the tariff bill, the Geneva negotiations, and our over-all trade policy in the near future.

January 27, 1977
Customs Tariff

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take up some of the remarks that my hon. colleague has already made. I think the House will understand our frustration in not being able to have what I would regard as a meaningful review of the total international picture surrounding Canada's trade with foreign nations, and the negotiations taking place in Geneva at the present time. While the minister referred to a debate last fall, he did not make it clear that that debate was triggered by this party using an opposition day to get some insight into what was transpiring with regard to international trade matters. I would point out that the Minister of Finance, who is primarily responsible for and who directs what is happening in Geneva, did not enter that debate. We still have not heard what he believes to be Canada's current position in the Geneva negotiations.
In short, Mr. Chairman, I believe there is an element of frustration here and that somehow the minister should try to relieve that frustration this evening by giving us at least a brief outline of what he feels the current stance is in the Canadian negotiations in Geneva, where he sees the problems, and where we might be making some headway. Before we get into the provisions of Bill C-15, I would hope that the minister, having failed to make any further comments at the conclusion of second reading, would at least review some of the comments made in the dozen or so speeches given on second reading.
The minister says that he hopes the bill will get speedy passage. I would remind all hon. members that it is not the opposition which has delayed the legislation. This bill has lain on the order paper for three months without being brought forward. Surely, 25 minutes after the bill coming up again for consideration after that three months delay, and the opposition not having delayed second reading, we should be entitled to some explanation on these two broad matters-first what the over-all stance is at the present time and the degree of success or failure we are meeting in Geneva and, second, a reply to some of the points raised in the dozen or so speeches on second reading.
Perhaps I could summarize our frustration this way, Mr. Chairman. This is literally the only jurisdiction in the democratic world, as far as I can make out, where there is no meaningful review of what our trade negotiators do when they enter the GATT negotiations. In the United States an act was passed through Congress which sets guidelines for the subsequent negotiations. They have an ongoing committee to review the GATT negotiations. Yet we in this House are asked to respond after decisions are made; we are asked to respond, for example, to a bill such as Bill C-15 after the government has decided to change tariffs in whatever way it sees fit.
We are frustrated because the Finance Committee of this House has been virtually idle during the second session of this parliament. We have done virtually nothing in that committee because, for some reason or other, the minister is not inclined to expedite business to the committee or even to appear, in the case of Bill C-5, to enable the bill to be continued with.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They have to get through second reading in order to get to committee.

The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance says they have to get to committee. I would point out that this bill is before us in Committee of the Whole and we are asking the minister for comment on the subjects to which I have referred. Bill C-5 has been before the Finance Committee for some time and we cannot get the minister to appear so that we may have the benefit of his comments.
In short, Mr. Chairman, and following on the comments of my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton West, I feel that it is very much in the interest of members of the House that the minister comment on the two subjects that have been raised. Certainly he need not be frightened that the bill is going to be delayed. It is a short bill. But he should take the opportunity to give members a little insight into what is happening in these rather secretive discussions in Geneva, and give the members who have raised questions on second reading the benefit of his comments.

Mr. Chairman, to deal with a couple of points raised by the hon. member, it is quite true that it was on an opposition day that hon. members opposite raised the question of trade policy. They raised it at a time when obligations outside this House prevented me from participating fully in the debate, but the government position was very ably set forth on that day by my parliamentary secretary.
Hear, hear!

He was ably supported by the hon. member for Eglinton who has had extensive experience, as a Privy Councillor and before that as a public servant, with this type of negotiation.
With regard to the business of the House, as the hon. member knows, Bill C-5 is companion to the bill to amend the Bretton-Woods Agreements Act. I would be delighted to move the Bretton-Woods Agreements Act to the committee and talk about international monetary policy, but people in Canada are waiting for this budget legislation to be enacted. The priority for the House is the budget. We have spent over a week on second reading and on the committee stage of the income tax bill, and two full days of debate on second reading with regard to the customs tariff. The time that hon. members choose to take on these budget bills is not only prejudicial to people like pork producers and others but is making it difficult to get on with the heavy agenda of the House.
I feel I would be trespassing on the rule of relevance if I started a long dissertation on the subject of Canada's trade policy. We have a specific bill on which we have had extensive discussion in the budget debate, so I think I should confine my remarks to the terms of this bill and not go into the broader questions that hon. members would like to have canvassed.

Mr. Chairman, I fully endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Edmonton West and the hon. member for York Simcoe. I find it a little odd that the minister should say now that we have to rush this bill through, especially since the last time we debated it was October 28. For almost three months he has had it in his back pocket.
January 27, 1977
You filibustered it.
Not us.

I think that if the speeches that we made, in which we pointed out to the government our point of view, were of such a nature that the minister was sensitive about them so that he now wants to call it a filibuster and does not want the other side of the story told, nor does he want to listen to the opposition and to what the people of Canada are saying, and therefore has not brought it back to the House for three months, and now that he has brought it in wants to rush it through, then it is just too bad. I did hope he would have something to say about the textile industry. Things have happened in that industry between the time of the debate on October 28 last and now, and he has not given us any explanation on that.
Nevertheless, I should like to ask the minister some questions about a subject that has been dear to me and about which I have asked question of several ministers of finance ever since I have been here. It concerns the customs tariff on small packages of pesticide. I received a letter from the minister on March 24, 1976, in which he said that his officials were looking at it and that consideration would be given to the matter in the budget. We are now debating the customs tariff changes proposed in the budget that was brought down on March 25 but nothing was done this time, as in the past, nor have I had any explanation as to why something is not being done about this.
I should like to ask the minister a specific question about tariff item 69605-1-scientific apparatus, etc.
That is in clause 3.
Mr. Chairman, I am advised that this is in clause 3, so I will wait.

As the Minister of Finance is aware, considerable attention was devoted by the Minister of National Revenue to a matter of customs and tariffs regarding groceries, because many Canadian shoppers are going down to Bellingham in the United States and as far south as Seattle to do their shopping. On these shopping trips anomalies in prices become very obvious to shoppers.
I should like to have an explanation of one of these anomalies. Can the minister give me the reason for this? I know many people who would appreciate it. For example, cookies that are baked in my riding neighbouring on the U.S. border sell for 30 cents to 40 cents a pound less in the United States than they do in the very locality where they are baked. Why do they cost less after having been exported to the U.S. than they do right in Canada where they are baked?

With regard to the question of pesticides, that matter was canvassed in the community at the time in preparation for the budget, and I can say to the hon. gentleman that objections were raised by a number of Canadi-
Customs Tariff
an producers with regard to a change in this tariff item. It was on the basis of these objections that we concluded we should not make a change at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I was wondering, with regard to the remarks of the minister as they related to the pork industry, whether I understood him correctly that he would be dealing with that matter in the proposed budget.

No, Sir. What I said was that as soon as the bill is passed I will be able to exercise the powers given under the bill to restore the level of protection which, under the bill, was to be reduced. This will be done as a result of representations from the pork producers. We do not have to wait for the budget, but by executive order I would be in a position to do that.
I cannot give an explanation for the marketing practices or the differences in cost on one or the other side of the border. I would point out, however, that item number 63500-1 does reduce the level of protection on biscuits on re-importation to Canada. I cannot explain the specific marketing situation of that commodity in the lower mainland and in northern Washington.

The minister has used the word "producers". He said that some producers were against it. I wonder if he would clarify that. Does he mean producers of agricultural products who use the pesticide, or pesticide producers?
I mean the chemical manufacturers in Canada.

May I make an observation on that? The people who want this tariff removed are the producers of food who use pesticides to produce food and who have very little, if any, tariff on their products. Take, for instance, apples. There is free trade on apples in Canada. If we are not going to protect our agricultural producers to any degree, then why should the manufacturers of products which they use get protection?

I would remind the hon. member that there is a reference now before the tariff board on fresh fruits and vegetables. The board will be reporting some time during the course of this year. On all these matters it is a trade-off between the interests of different economic groups. In this case we are also looking at the jobs of people employed in chemical manufacturing.

On clause 1, which is general, I should like to inquire whether the minister and his department have given any consideration to the practice which seems to be prevalent in the United States and which might be described as internal dumping. I have an example which has been brought to my attention of a kind of motor that is used in powering large model aeroplanes, model railways, and other models of different kinds. This is a hobby, but it has become a very large one, and the total sum of money spent on these machines is very large. They are not manufactured in Canada and, because

January 27, 1977
Customs Tariff
there is a lack of any kind of protection, they cannot really be manufactured here. The distributors who have been importing them find themselves at a disadvantage because they must pay tariff on what is known as a fair trade price.
Having done that, and having brought in supplies, they find to their amazement that the stock they bring in simply becomes an opportunity for would-be purchasers to view the stock and make up their minds about it. They, in turn, can phone to the United States through a zenith number and order the same item for delivery by direct mail from a discount house at a considerably reduced price, a lower price than one on which the distributor would have paid duty. When the item comes to the customs office in Canada, a purchaser pays the duty on the lower price and makes a saving. He is not required to pay the provincial sales tax, and so makes a further saving.
One distributor was in a very difficult position. In order to improve his situation he developed a repair service for these machines, and in a sense that kept the loyalty of his customers, until he was charged duty on the parts he had to import to do the repair work, a service which could not otherwise be provided in Canada. What was developing as a Canadian industry was placed in jeopardy because there was no protection. If Canadian technicians can repair the machines, they can also manufacture them. That is one more example of moving into manufacturing small articles which require a great deal of technical skill, which we have here, but it is not possible because there is no tariff protection.
There are a couple of specific items which I would like to bring to the minister's attention. Is any consideration being given by the federal customs office to collecting provincial sales tax? A person who spoke to me said that otherwise the federal customs office would become a retailer in competition with retailers in the area. Are any moves being made to raise a barrier against internal discounting, where the manufacturer, the wholesaler, and the discounter are all one business, all owned by the same people who, when their own market is saturated, sell to their own discount house, and through it peddle into Canada directly at a great advantage?

Mr. Chairman, on that kind of transaction where an individual imports, there is a less extensive regime for control than there is when there are imports of commercial scale. The law is the same, but for practical reasons it is not possible to apply it with the full severity which would be applicable in the case of a larger shipment.
The question of valuation is basically one for the Minister of National Revenue. Perhaps the hon. member would like to write to me about that particular point, and I would be quite happy to seek the advice of my colleague.
I make just one remark with regard to provincial sales tax. It may indeed be that individuals are not paying provincial sales tax on those items, but that is not because they are exempt by law; it is because of the practical problem of collecting it. They are, of course, obliged to pay the sales tax.

So far as the Department of Finance is concerned, we do not have any arrangements under consideration at the moment for mutual collection of taxes in this way, although again I would have to inquire of my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, to see if in her department such a regime is being contemplated.

Mr. Chairman, I was not here when the original debate on this bill took place, so I did not have the pleasure of hearing what was said. However, I gather the reason for these changes is to lower the tariff on certain items. Could the minister tell me what progress, if any, is being made, or is any attempt being made to negotiate lower tariffs on Canadian fish products in the European Common Market? Can he give me a report on that? Is an attempt being made, and what are the prospects of success? As the hon. gentleman knows, there is a considerable tariff on Canadian fish products going to Europe, and this is where we have to put some of our effort in the next three or four years.

The best description I can give to the hon. gentleman, who was not here at the earlier stages of the debate, is that this is a continuation of the reduction of tariffs on many consumer items imported into Canada, principally food items, for the purpose of the over-all anti-inflation campaign.
With regard to the negotiations at the Geneva round, I indicated to the hon. member for Edmonton West a moment ago that this might not be an appropriate discussion because it does not relate to this particular bill. However, I would be glad to discuss this with the hon. gentleman in the House at some future time.

Mr. Chairman, there is another matter which is a continual nuisance and grievance to sportsmen in the country, and that has to do with the need to import cartridges, primers, and charges for sport shooting. For skeet shooting especially a lot of ammunition is needed. Much of this material is no longer made in Canada. CIL does not manufacture it any more, so these sportsmen have to go to the United States to get their primers, and I suppose also the charges and cartridges. The main question in their minds is, why is there duty on them in the first place since they are not manufactured in Canada? It certainly cannot be a protective tariff, and I suppose we have to assume-and perhaps the minister can correct me on this-that it is a revenue producing tariff and that that is its only justification. At any rate there are many sportsmen who are wondering why there is this tariff since these items are not manufactured in Canada.
My second related question is, if there has to be a tariff, why are there three or four different scales of tariffs on the items? Why is it that on one item it is about 7.5 per cent and on another one 15 per cent? I believe the tariff is as high as 32 per cent on some of these items. If there has to be a tariff on these cartridges and primers, why can there not be an across the board tariff so that all they have to do is pay a fiat rate on this sports equipment? Why do there have to be excessive 30 per cent or 40 per cent tariffs on some of the items, since they
January 27, 1977

are not manufactured in Canada in the first place? It seems to me these people are being penalized because there is not an industry in Canada which will produce these items.

Mr. Chairman, I am reminded that the highest rate of tariff in Canada is about 20 per cent. There is a series of tariff items dealing with ammunition in a broader sense. It is not infrequent that with the shift in commercial competition, particular lines may be dropped. I suppose what the hon. member is really suggesting is that we should have separate tariff items for primers which, as he says-and I do not question him-are not manufactured in Canada, but of course there are other kinds of ammunition which are manufactured here, and it is to provide both actual protection and a protective opportunity to Canadian industry that the tariff item is there.
For those items which are not manufactured in Canada is it not possible to drop that tariff entirely?

I have not examined the individual items in detail, but it may well be that what the hon. gentleman is suggesting-that is, that those which are included in a broader item should be segregated out and, in effect, that a new item should be created-could be dealt with in the budget considerations which are now under way, and perhaps I could undertake to examine this particular question. If the hon. gentleman would let me have a more precise description of the various items and indicate those which, to his knowledge, are manufactured in Canada and those which are not, I would be delighted to examine them.
Will do.

Apparently the minister is disinclined to give us any explanation tonight concerning the pending or current negotiations in Geneva. I wonder if the minister could at least give us an undertaking that he will take up with the government House leader the possibility of having a reference of our trade negotiations as they now stand, with particular reference to what is happening in Geneva, to our Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs so that we may have a meaningful review of what the government is doing on behalf of Canada in Geneva.

I would be quite happy to discuss that with the government House leader. It is going to be an important consideration during 1977 as the tariff negotiations get under way again in Geneva. It may interest hon. members to know that the new United States Secretary of the Treasury was the prime negotiator for the United States at the Kennedy Round; in that sense I would look forward to an early meeting, to learn from him his approach to the Geneva round of negotiations.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister confirm that he is the minister in the government who has over-all
Customs Tariff
responsibility for the GATT negotiations, and that Mr. Gray asks him for instructions as to what action to take in Geneva?

Mr. Chairman, Mr. Gray, of course, was an official of my department. I would say that responsibility for the operation is shared by three departments: My own is the department responsible in particular fo the customs tariff; the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is responsible from the standpoint of Canada's over-all trade position and the position of Canadian industry; and the Department of External Affairs has responsibility for Canada's foreign relations. It is, therefore, not the decision of a single department; rather, the work of the government in this respect is co-ordinated primarily between those three departments. I would add that the Department of National Revenue is responsible for the practical application of the customs tariff which this parliament enacts; it also has other responsibilities. The anti-dumping tribunal reports through me to parliament, as does the Tariff Board. A number of different departments are affected in the government of Canada, and responsibility is shared among them in that way.
Mr. Chairman, are the items covered by Bill C-15 covered by the commodity coding system used by the Department of National Revenue?
Mr. Chairman, I cannot say if the answer is in the affirmative. I will look into it in the next few minutes.

Mr. Chairman, while I realize that various departments of government are involved in providing total input with regard to the GATT negotiations, I wonder if the minister can confirm or otherwise if his department co-ordinates the activities of the other departments and has the responsibility of handling the instructions and communications going to our negotiators in Geneva.

Mr. Chairman, it is not unique. For the reasons I have indicated, the responsibilities of several departments are involved in this. I do not think one can say, in respect of a day's operations at Geneva, that it is specifically the final responsibility of any one department; however, as Minister of Finance, for the reasons I have indicated, I have responsibility for the customs tariff; and the primary purpose of the Geneva round of course is to negotiate lower levels of tariff.

Mr. Chairman, may I draw the attention of the minister to tariff items 8717-1 and 8728-1, as referred to in clause 1 and schedule I. The first item mentioned deals with onions; they are to be allowed in free under the British preferential tariff; there is a tariff of 1.5 cents per pound under the most favoured nation tariff, and a tariff of 1.5 cents per pound under the general tariff. The second item to which I referred deals with green onions, and the tariffs set out are exactly the same, under those three headings. Is the minister familiar with the tariff charged by American authorities for comparable items? In short, we know from the schedule what
2472

January 27, 1977
Customs Tariff
tariff is charged against American goods entering this country. Can the minister say what tariffs the United States authorities charge on comparable goods entering that country?
Mr. Chairman, we do not have the American tariff at hand. Of course we are now looking at the Canadian tariff, but I would be prepared to get that information for the hon. member.

I always like to be helpful, Mr. Chairman. I have the American tariff before me; it happens to be 1.75 cents per pound. Consequently I understand that our bags of onions entering the United States face a tariff of 87.5 cents, whereas, in accordance with the tariff we are now considering, the total tariff we shall charge with respect to American produce entering this country will be 75 cents per bag. Therefore there is a differential of 12.5 cents weighted against the Canadian producer of onions. I wonder if the minister would indicate why there is this discrepancy?

Mr. Chairman, I cannot really give the hon. gentleman an explanation of why the rates would not match. I notice that we have made some sales in the American market in recent years although, for obvious reasons, the nature of our climate and the fact that our growing season is short, the volume of produce from Canada going to the United States market is very much smaller then that coming in the other direction.

Mr. Chairman, has the minister discussed with or had overtures from the onion producers of Canada, more particularly the onion producers of Ontario, who have indicated to me that they would like to see parity between American and Canadian tariffs since this would enable them to be more competitive in the U.S. market.

Mr. Chairman, this is one of the items in the fruit and vegetable reference which is now before the Tariff Board. With regard to specific changes proposed, the Canadian Horticultural Council did not oppose the original reduction after the February 19, 1973, budget, although the council did oppose the reduction proposed in the November 18, 1974, budget, and offered to provide additional information on the subject. No further representations have been forthcoming since that offer.

Mr. Chairman, this is a most important matter to the 300 Ontario onion growers who this year alone will produce nearly three million bags of onions. Could the minister indicate whether those tariff items which we are now considering could be altered, if a fair case were to be made for the alteration, despite their passage in their present form, say this evening? I understand that our producers would like something to happen. They want to see the Americans lower their duty to the Canadian level; or they want us to raise our tariff to the American tariff level; or, third, they are in favour of both tariffs being abolished entirely. In short, it is apparent that our producers are confident that they can compete and, if the tariff barrier could be removed, they could stand American

competition and even tap the American market and, hopefully, expand those trade figures to which reference has already been made.

Mr. Chairman, several stages will have to be gone through. Of course the purpose of the fruit and vegetable reference is to determine better the impact on the Canadian market of the tariffs in question; this would affect not only consumers but, of course, Canadian producers. Second, on the basis of the results of the Tariff Board examination, this could well be a matter for negotiation in the Kennedy Round. However, I would say that the question of agriculture has not yet been broached in the Kennedy Round negotiations. One could almost say it has been so important and critical between the major trading partners that it has not been approached, but it will obviously have to be, to bring that negotiation to a finish.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask the minister a question with regard to a similar problem. It relates to flax, a crop grown in a relatively small area of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and the Dakotas. There is a 50 cent duty on flax moving into the United States. I understand there is no duty on flax coming into Canada from the United States. This is a small crop in terms of volume, a few million bushels. The price in the two countries is generally the same, but conditions such as shipping orders and so on make a difference. I believe the flax producers have asked that the 50 cents a bushel tariff on Canadian flax going to the United States be removed or at least equalized. If possible, it would be preferable to remove it. Perhaps the minister can make some comment on this.

Mr. Chairman, that would be a subject for negotiation when the agricultural items come up before the Geneva round. If I could just refer to the question asked by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth, I take it the question refers to the Statistics Canada commodity codes in this respect. The items here would be covered by the commodity codes. These items are rather narrower in definition generally speaking than the broader commodity codes, but the commodity codes obviously would cover these.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know them as Statistics Canada commodity codes, only National Revenue because National Revenue produces a catalogue. It is a little more detailed than Statistics Canada commodity codes.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister can inform us if the Horticultural Association made any representation regarding imports from Taiwan and Korea on such items as mushrooms, wax beans, and green beans. The price level at which these products are coming into Canada is destroying the agricultural economy. Certainly on the west coast it is really hurting it. Will the minister inform us whether there has been any representation by the Horticultural Association on that tariff item?

My second question is with regard to an arrangement between Canada and the United States on the matter of potatoes. The minister can correct me if I am wrong. Under the GATT agreement there is a kind of reciprocating tariff arrangement between Canada and the United States on potatoes. The quota for Canadian shipments into the United States is really quite low. The American quota for shipping into Canada is really quite high. Regardless of the percentage rate of the tariff, it is really a restrictive tariff for Canadian potatoes to be shipped into the United States. However, the Americans can ship high volumes from Idaho and Washington. With their mass production and corporate farming they can inundate the Canadian market and are doing so, mostly with their cull potatoes. They can sell high grade potatoes on the market in the United States, take their culls and literally dump them in Canada, ruining the Canadian potato industry in British Columbia. Can the minister give some answers on that?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is quite right. The Canadian market is more open than the American one in the sense that we have a much less restrictive quota. Again, this is something which is under consideration, the fresh fruit and vegetable reference. On the question of representations with regard to mushrooms, this has been a matter of substantial representation. 1 would have to check the record to see if the Canadian Horticultural Association itself actually made the representation. I certainly know that others have. I can also check the record with regard to wax beans.

Are there definite plans for changing the agreement with the United States on the matter of export and import potatoes so that the Canadian potato industry will have a little more protection from the American high volume?
Not until we have the assessment of the Tariff Board. Of course it would be appropriate to do it within the context of the Geneva round.

Mr. Chairman, if I could go back to my questioning with regard to onions, will the minister indicate to us exactly what we can do here tonight? As I understand it, the onion producers are saying that there are three alternatives-let us have both nations go down to zero, let us have the Americans reduce their tariff to our level or, alternatively, increase our tariff one and one half cents to the American level. Can we tonight actually amend the tariff to go to the American level, or is this subject to the GATT negotiations?
Mr. Chairman, that is a bound tariff under the GATT.

Mr. Chairman, there are two more items about which I would like to ask the minister. One is the matter of fresh lettuce. There is a tariff arrangement between Canada and the United States on this matter. However, all too often the tariff is imposed when it is almost too late to save the Canadian market. The low tariff on the American or Mexican
Customs Tariff
product coming into Canada stays on just long enough until the Canadian product is coming on the market. By that time it is too late to save the Canadian market. The protection does not come on in time. Since there are different marketing conditions and weather conditions, for example, between the west coast industry and Ontario, would it be possible to have the regional tariffs come in at different times of the year and let the local boards adjust those tariffs so that they would be sensitive to the marketing conditions of their areas and thereby protect the farmers in particular localities?
My second question relates to frozen vegetables. Food processors on the west coast in particular have a high inventory of frozen vegetables. It will be almost impossible to market them by the time the next crop comes on stream because of the competition from the United States. Is something going to be done with regard to tariffs on processed vegetables, especially in the frozen state, in order to protect the jobs of Canadians, not only in the farming industry but in the food processing industry?

Mr. Chairman, there is a regional variation under the tariff arrangements with regard to fresh fruits and vegetables. For example, the hon. member for York-Simcoe was referring to onions under item 8717-1. Lettuce is not mentioned in this bill, but there are variations between the maritimes, eastern Ontario and Quebec, and the Lakehead and West. So there is a wide scope for regional variation. The hon. member will note that a number of items refer to frozen vegetables of various kinds and there is some reduction in the tariff. As I said earlier on, it has been in effect on a temporary basis for a number of years.
Could lettuce be included in that regional variation?
It is.

Mr. Chairman, could the minister give us an estimate of the impact of these tariff changes, particularly with respect to the British preferential tariff and the most favoured nation tariff, on the general system of preferences, since the two are related? I am thinking particularly of some of the items I see listed on page 13-typewriters, typewriter parts, spectacles and eye-glasses, carpet sweepers, electric vacuum cleaners and attachments, and so on. The list includes power lawn mowers, electric irons, electric lamps, electric lamp fixtures and so on. In other words, there is a range of manufactured items not only in the electrical manufacturing field but in other secondary industry. I ask this question in light of the fact that the general system of preferences grants to the developing countries-that is, the non-Commonwealth countries-the British preference or the most favoured nation tariff less one-third. Thus, if we are changing these tariffs we are also changing the level of the general system of preferences.
It is very difficult to follow from the tables provided here what change is granted under, say, the British preference and

January 27, 1977
Customs Tariff
therefore, by extension, what is granted to the developing countries. I ask this question particularly in the light of the shrinking employment picture in some of our industries, especially the electrical manufacturing industry.

Mr. Chairman, I am not sure I fully grasped the hon. gentleman's question but I can say that the general system of preferences is unaffected by the bill before us. The preferences as given under the general system are either one-third off the most favoured nation rate or the British preferential rate, whichever is the lower. Without these particular reductions the MFN or BP rate would apply, so the general system of preferences will, speaking generally, be more favourable to developing countries which are entitled to it than the BP rate on the same commodity.

Would the minister comment upon the effect of clause 5(3) on section 1 of the act? I ask this because he may recall that the effect of section 1 is that those changes in the tariff in the items outlined in subsection (1) will continue until June 30, 1977, that is to say, they will expire in approximately five months. The rates then go back to those which prevailed on February 20, 1973, and as of July 1, unless something is done in the next budget, the rates will revert to those of February 20, 1973. Perhaps the minister's director of tariffs can tell us in reference to all these items which appear in schedules I, II and III whether the rates were higher or lower, or is there an evening off?
I am advised that it only applied to Schedule I and that the rates were higher.
Therefore as of July 1, 1977, the effective rates will be higher?
Unless further action is taken in the meantime, it will be higher.

Mr. Chairman, returning to item 8717-1, it appears that we cannot tonight amend the bill and that if this is to be changed it will have to be changed in the current negotiations in Switzerland. Could the minister indicate what ongoing discussions take place with respect to this type of item, fruits and vegetables generally, to ensure that there is a proper understanding between our negotiators and those who are actually in the business of producing these items in Canada, as negotiations continue in Geneva?

Apart from the representations from organizations such as the Canadian Horticultural Council, to which I have referred, there is of course the ongoing work of the Canadian Tariffs and Trade Committee which has been engaged in cross-country contact with regard to the reduction of items in the Geneva negotiations.

Would the minister give the House an undertaking that he would inquire of those two bodies as to the current feeling with respect to the tariff on onions as I understand there is quite a serious problem, especially for Ontario onion growers, at the present time? I feel that what-
(Mr. O'Connell.]
ever benefit their thinking can bring should be available to our negotiators in Geneva.
Yes, Mr. Chairman.

Perhaps I can move on to another item under clause 1-number 9800-1, bananas. Can the minister tell us where the bulk of our bananas come from? I notice there is a free tariff with regard to British preferential countries and most favoured nations, but the general tariff is a dollar per hundred pounds.
The bulk of the bananas we import comes from MFN countries, in particular, Costa Rica, Equador and the Honduras.

Mr. Chairman, there is a further item I should like to question. It is 92942-4-caffein and its salts. This is free under the British preferential tariff, 10 per cent under the most favoured nation and 25 per cent under the general tariff. Would the minister indicate where the imports of caffein and its salts come from? The item is on page 18, 92942-4.
The bulk of the imports come from the European Economic Community. The source is not segregated as countries.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 2 agreed to.
On clause 3-Schedule A further amended.

In connection with this clause, Mr. Chairman, there has been a great deal of correspondence with the minister. I know that many of my colleagues like the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre- anyone indeed, who represents a riding in a city in which there is a university-
Hear, hear!

-has received extensive correspondence regarding item 69605-1. It arises out of the bulletin which was issued by the Department of National Revenue with regard to the very narrow interpretation being used. I do not know whether, as a result of representations, the bulletin has been suspended. If the minister looks at the item on page 22, in the middle of the item there is reference to "preparations", and then follows the change "including containers in which imported, for use directly in research". The word "teaching" has been dropped.
I have before me a letter from a professor of surgery in the Department of Surgery of the University of Alberta. I have other letters from the Department of Chemistry of the University of Alberta, from Calgary and many other places. The first letter to which I referred has this to say in part:
Many departments in this University maintain stores of scientific supplies and this is necessary in view of the lengthy delays often encountered in obtaining items ordered from the scientific supply houses. While much of these stocked
January 27, 1977

supplies go towards research work, some are used in teaching. Since, in fact, it is very difficult to separate out the teaching and research functions of a University it will not be possible to prepare the required statements for the tariff exemption.
For example, the Health Sciences Animal Centre in my Faculty uses some $60,000/annum worth of specialized animal feeds. While the overwhelming majority of the animals are used in research, some are used in teaching. With some hundred scientific investigators using the facilities of the Centre for an even larger number of projects, honest production of the descriptions of the research and use of the prepared feed will just not be possible. The result will be about a 30 per cent rise in animal feed costs or $20,000/year raising animal charges to users about 20 per cent.
I have another letter from the Department of Chemistry of the University of Alberta which states that this change will cost them $64,000 a year more. The same figures are given by Calgary and Manitoba.
I also have a letter written by the minister which says this, in part:
I appreciate that this amendment is causing problems for universities, hospitals and their suppliers of preparations. Officials in my Department are discussing this matter with officials in the Department of National Revenue who are responsible for the administration of this provision.
A meeting was also held recently between officials in my Department, the Department of National Revenue and representatives of the universities. It was agreed that the administration of the new provision would be re-examined. My officials will report back to me shortly at which time I will be in a better position to decide whether a further amendment to the item will be necessary.
I await the answer, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, to complete the public record on this, the item in question was affected by a Tariff Board decision rendered in July, 1976, and the new provision has been much more restrictive than was intended by the government. I would therefore be proposing to take action to give it the less restrictive meaning that was originally intended and for this purpose to seek a remission order pursuant to section 17 of the Financial Administration Act.

May I ask specifically how the minister intends to proceed? The wording is there and the word "teaching" no longer applies. I assume the effect of the Tariff Board decision was that the exemption be applied only to those materials that go into research. It is true that the minister can take, shall we say, compensating action, but it must be done in two ways. First of all, the item has to be amended, I think, in order, shall we say, to eliminate the effect of the Tariff Board decision; otherwise the Department of National Revenue will have to carry on. Secondly, for this year, or whenever the amendment might come in, the minister is going to take the remission procedure.
If he follows the remission route it is going to be a real headache for everyone concerned. The paperwork involved is out of this world. Universities and hospitals complain that to keep track of these preparations and foods, and so on, for animals either used in research or in teaching, it will cost so much in paperwork alone plus, of course, the duty that will have to be paid. If they are to go along the remission route they will be required to apply to the Department of National Revenue for reimbursement of the amount they have had to pay.
Customs Tariff
It may be that the Department of National Revenue has suspended collection, but I do not know what route can be used by those people who, unfortunately, have to be put through this bureaucratic grist mill as a result of the Tariff Board interpretation.

Mr. Chairman, as I have said, this can be achieved by remission at this point. To complete discussions for our next budget in several months' time, we hope to propose wording which will be mutually satisfactory to all concerned and which would provide the ongoing assurance that a less restrictive interpretation will be given. Therefore I propose to recommend to the Governor in Council that remissions be available in the interim until there is some agreement on the most effective wording to attain the objective that we set out to attain.
In other words, for the time being we will have to wear the hair shirt?
For the time being you will have to wear the hair shirt, recovering some of the hair afterwards.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 4-Schedule C amended.

Mr. Chairman, because of the peculiar wording of Schedule IV, referred to in clause 4, I was wondering whether we could have some explanation from the minister. Item 99206-1 reads:
Goods manufactured or produced wholly or in part by prison labour, unless in any particular case or class of cases exempted from the provisions of this item by a regulation of the Governor in Council.

Mr. Chairman, this item now prohibits the importation of all goods produced by prison labour unless exempted by the Governor in Council for further manufacture in Canada. The item is being amended to allow the Governor in Council to exempt goods from prohibition in other circumstances and we are attempting to simplify the wording at the same time.
Two cases where it might be considered desirable to have prohibition are when they are being imported for public exhibition, or when Canadians return from visits to other countries having purchased goods of this kind without knowledge of the prohibition or the fact that the goods have been made by prisoners.
I should explain that the item was introduced in the late nineteenth century, and it appears that the item was designed at the time to protect Canadian manufacturers from imports of goods produced by cheap prison labour. It was amended in 1953 to allow the Governor in Council to import exempt goods when they were required for further manufacture. However, no exemption of this kind has in fact ever been made.
That is the basic background. Some people may be inadvertently importing into Canada goods of this kind-inadvertently in the sense of not knowing they were produced by prison labour, or for public exhibition-and this gives the Governor

Customs Tariff
in Council the opportunity to make those exceptions from the general prohibition.

The minister says "for public exhibition". I just do not follow what are the circumstances under which we would want to have goods coming in which have been produced by prison labour. What type of exhibition is the minister referring to?

Handicrafts, paintings, works of art of that kind which may have been produced by prison labour in other countries and originally imported into Canada. It may be a rather esoteric interest on someone's part, but one cannot tell; there may be an artistic genius currently reposing in custody.
From the practical standpoint, Mr. Chairman, would the minister indicate to what extent these goods are inadvertently, as the minister says, imported by these unsuspecting souls?
There have been cases, I am advised, but I am sorry, the actual figures are not available.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 5-Commencement.

Mr. Chairman, I might just indicate that hon. members will have noticed that when introduced at the first reading stage, the bill had a number of blank statements in it, both in clause 5 (2) and Schedule I. I would like to suggest that it might be appropriate that they be filled in for this purpose. My understanding is that the suggestion from the Chair is that they could be treated as corrections of a typographical error, but perhaps you could advise me on that, Mr. Chairman.

speechtext: I do not see any difficulty if the committee agrees, otherwise we would have to do it by amendment. What date is the hon. minister suggesting? Is it the date of first reading?
October 14, 1976.

Under the circumstances, Mr. Chairman, we might agree to this as long as it does not serve as a precedent. It could have been the 14th day of October, 19, and then blank. Then, of course, we could insert years, and that could hardly be considered a minor correction. I can readily understand why October 14 is included, but I would not like this procedure to be used as a precedent, particularly if the gap were to come expressed as a month or year.

Agreed.
On Schedule I.

Mr. Chairman, as the minister has indicated, the items I specifically referred to, 8717-1 and 8728-1, are in fact unamendable in that they are subject to an international agreement. I was wondering whether the minister would indicate if there are any items in this schedule that are amendable, or are they all structured in that way and only changeable as a result of negotiation in Geneva?

Indeed, you could go back through these particular items and find they are bound items back to February 14, 1973. The hon. gentleman's question was with regard to a basic amendment that was in force. The basic tariff provision that was in force on that particular day was a bound tariff under GATT. This particular bill substantially reduces from that bound level to a lower level. Of course, we could by amendment this evening increase them. We could, with appropriate amendments to the ways and means resolution, increase the tariff protection again up to the February 14, 1973, level.

I am somewhat puzzled by the minister's answer to my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe. Surely it is open to an hon. member to amend a taxing statute providing he reduces the amount of the tax. We have done that on a number of occasions. It seems to me that also, subject to I suppose what might be an agreement, there could be other amendments. The government did not seem to be bothered a few years ago during the Kennedy Round agreements having regard to negotiated reductions in tariffs on industrial chemicals. The former minister, Mr. Benson, telescoped three or four years into one in the second year of the phased reductions on industrial chemicals as a step to combat inflation, making things cheaper on the domestic market. The phasing was dropped very quickly for those years.
The government took that action and it was subject to an agreement that it would be for five years. How does the government then suggest it has the power to change unilaterally the agreement, while a member cannot? If that is the case and it is proper for the government, then surely it would be open to a member here to make a proposal which, if the House agrees, would provide for a unilateral change. I would like to hear an explanation. I may be wrong in my logic, but if the government has the power to amend unaliterally an international agreement like that, surely this House, on the proposal of an hon. member to do the same thing, would have the same sort of power to do precisely the same thing.
January 27, 1977

I am not sure that we are addressing ourselves to the same thing. The hon. gentleman has suggested as one alternative increasing the Canadian tariff on onions. It was in that particular circumstance that I indicated this is one of the rates that had been brought down in February, 1973, which we could move back up again by executive order.

Mr. Chairman, this is one matter I have not been able to check. I have not looked through the list thoroughly, but I do not seem to find any items relating for example to wheelchairs or any other equipment for paraplegics in any of the schedules. Could the minister give us some indication as to whether these are dutiable items and, if they are, whether it would be the fair, equitable and honourable thing to do if we removed these items?

I am advised, Mr. Chairman, that quite a few of the items sui generis such as wheelchairs referred to by the hon. gentleman are now duty free. Some of them bear a tariff up to a maximum of 10 per cent, so there are some of these devices still in that category. The reason, of course, is that there are some Canadian manufacturers in this area, and it will represent in a particular case a judgment as to whether that protection should be taken off in the interests of those with an affliction.

Agreed.
Schedule I agreed to.
On Schedule II.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw the attention of the committee to item no. 40964-1 which appears at the bottom of page 19 in Schedule II, electric or radio apparatus designed to identify livestock and record their consumption of feed on an individual basis and parts thereof. speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-21, to amend the Excise Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in introducing this bill I would remind the hon. members that my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), tabled a document entitled "An Energy Strategy for Canada-Policies for Self-reliance" in April of this year. In this document the government stated its objective of energy self-reliance, indicated a series of specific energy targets, and enumerated nine policy elements and priorities. These priorities included appropriate energy pricing, increased exploration and development, increased research and development and energy conservation. One of our goals is to reduce the average rate of growth of energy use in Canada over the next ten years. Energy conservation initiatives, including both tax incentives and tax penalties, form an important part of the government's policy of energy self-reliance.
This bill provides for the removal of federal sales tax from a number of items which contribute to the conservation of energy and to the development of new sources of energy. Included in this list are such items as solar furnaces and heating panels, heat pumps and wind-powered generating equipment. The current exemption for thermal insulation materials for buildings is extended to include thermal insulation materials designed for use in the insulation of pipes and ducts in buildings and mechanical systems.
The purpose of the removal of federal sales tax from the items referred to above is to promote the conservation of energy by encouraging the use of higher efficiency heating equipment, increased use of thermal insulation to reduce heat loss, and the development and application of new equipment designed to derive energy from other non-traditional sources. Provision is also made for the Governor in Council to prescribe, by regulation, additional equipment, articles or materials to be energy conservation equipment exempt from federal sales tax. This provision will facilitate prompt action to provide relief from tax when new items which can contribute to Canada's over-all energy conservation program become available on the Canadian market.
The bill also contains measures to deter wasteful energy consumption by increasing the special excise taxes on high

January 27, 1977
Excise Tax Act
energy-consuming vehicle and by imposing a new special excise tax on automotive air conditioners. The weight threshold above which the tax takes effect is reduced to 4,425 pounds for automobiles and to 5,000 pounds for station wagons and vans. In addition, the rates of tax applicable to vehicles which exceed their respective weight limits are increased to $30 for the first 100 pounds, $40 for the second 100 pounds, $50 for the third 100 pounds, and $60 for each additional 100 pounds in excess of the weight limit. The purpose of the tax is not to raise revenue but rather to encourage Canadians to demand, and the auto industry to produce, lighter, more energy-efficient cars.
In this regard, the ways and means motion tabled at the time of the May 25, 1976, budget provided for progressive reductions in the weight threshold with the result that, under a mature system, taxes amounting to as much as $1,000 would be imposed on the largest cars weighing approximately 5,300 pounds. Since the budget I have met with representatives of the auto industry and officials of my department have held extensive discussions with these representatives. Indeed, some discussions have been going on as a result with my colleagues, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and their officials with respect to this energy incentives tax. As a result of these discussions the government has been persuaded that an alternative form of tax based on vehicle fuel consumption rather than weight should be explored further by the industry and those within the government with responsibility for energy conservation.
To provide sufficient time for an in-depth study of this alternative, it was decided that the impact of the proposed tax changes should be reduced. For this reason the bill provides for a reduction of 75 pounds in the automobile weight limit and a reduction of 100 pounds in the weight limit for station wagons and vans, rather than the reductions of 250 and 350 pounds respectively proposed in the May 25 budget speech. The reductions in the weight limits and the increases in rate of tax applicable to vehicles in excess of the weight limits are effective as of September 1, 1976.
The further reductions in the weight threshold proposed in the May budget to come into effect in 1977 through 1979 will not be implemented at this time. I lay some stress on the words "at this time" because the one-year adaptation of the new rule was made specifically on the understanding that efforts would be made to move to the alternative means of gauging and preserving further energy consumption. I have left myself room for action in the current year, if there is no progress in this regard, to bring back measures like those originally proposed in the budget speech or, alternatively, one which would seem to be most effective to achieve the same end.
While the changes initially proposed will not be proceeded with in the current year it has really been a question of time to enable those concerned with this question to put into place proposals with respect to an alternative method of gauging energy conservation. The significant deterrent to the purchase and hence the production of energy-inefficient automobiles

which we have in mind will be implemented following completion of the joint government/industry study of a more effective method of implementing the policy. These will be complementary to the fleet-weighted mileage requirements announced earlier this year by my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
Mr. Speaker, the amendment pertaining to the special $100 dollar excise tax on air conditioners for cars, station-wagons, vans and light trucks is another measure to promote energy conservation. Automobile air conditioners have a marked effect on gas consumption, either directly, by using the car engine as power source or, indirectly, by adding weight to the vehicle. Studies show that in the case of heavy cars made in Canada and equipped with air conditioners, there is an average annual increase of 4 to 6 per cent of gas consumption as compared to that of similar vehicles without conditioners. In the case of smaller vehicles, gas consumption can go up by as much as 20 per cent if the car is equipped with an air conditioner.
On a technical point of view, the bill provides for a tax at the wholesale level so that taxpayers holding wholesale licences can buy merchandise subject to the excise tax without having to pay that tax when purchasing the goods. They are then required to pay the tax when they sell the goods, just as wholesalers holding licences must nowadays pay the sales tax on goods subject to the federal sales tax. This measure would cut down the administrative costs of taxpayers who previously had to fill out reimbursement claims since they are buying goods subject to an excise tax and which can be sold tax free. [English]
Mr. Speaker, after these brief words of introduction let me say in conclusion that the bill provides for important new measures to supplement those already in place to encourage greater conservation of energy by Canadians by penalizing wasteful or less essential uses of our energy resources, and by encouraging the development and the use of energy sources other than the scarce fossil fuels. Mr. Speaker, there is very little time left to me before the adjournment tonight, and I know that my colleagues tomorrow will talk on various subjects as they arise.
