speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: FISHERIES-PROPOSED PLAN FOR COMPENSATION FOR FISHERMEN ENGAGED IN REDFISH FISHERY-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to protest a cruel and inhumane lack of action by the government in a matter that seriously affects the province of Newfoundland. On December 10, 48 days ago, I asked a question about the fish docks available for fishing operations on the south coast of Newfoundland in the district of Burin-Burgeo for the owners of those plants who were having great difficulties because of their inability to catch fish under last year's quota system with their side trawlers.
I asked the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) a question on that and whether he was going to develop a plan to compensate them for their loss, because the lack of fish is not their fault but the fault of the government of Canada which, for years, was negligent in protecting that resource. He gave an unsatisfactory answer. He said he had no special assistance program. It appears he is going to do nothing. But 48 days later, on Monday, January 31, the fish plant at Gaultois in Burin-Burgeo, the district of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), will close with a loss of jobs for 220 men because the government has failed to take any action in the last 48 days to amend the new fishery management plan of the Minister of Fisheries, announced in December, so that they can catch fish with their side trawlers and keep the plant in operation, or give it special financial assistance for the same purpose.
The plant at Gaultois lost over $400,000 in the last quarter of 1976. The Minister of Fisheries was informed that that plant would not be able to operate at the end of the month if no special assistance program was brought about. He was informed of that in a wire on January 13, and in a wire dated December 24 the owner of the fish plant at Ramea, Mrs. Margaret Penney, wired the Minister of Fisheries about the conditions in the plant at Ramea and about its losses in the fall of 1976 because of the lack of quotas and the difficulty with side trawlers. She advised that it was likely she would have to close and that another 375 jobs would be gone in Ramea if no steps were taken by the Government of Canada. At the plant in Gaultois only 55,000 pounds of fillets were processed in December, and in the other two months, October and November, only 150,000 pounds were processed, when the normal production is 400,000. They are losing a fortune because they cannot catch fish. They cannot absorb these losses, yet in the fishery management plan the minister announced in December no specific provisions were made for side trawlers or for these plants on the south coast.
What is the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the member of parliament for that area, doing about that? He was in Newfoundland over the Christmas period for two weeks, yet no special federal help has come. These plants are all in his constituency. He did not even have a meeting on the subject. We know that he has been gone for the last two weeks on official business in South America, and he got back only
2480

Adjournment Debate
yesterday, but what has the Minister of Fisheries been doing in his absence? Is the fishing industry on the south coast of Newfoundland going to be allowed to collapse because the Minister of Fisheries is, for some reason, unable to amend his fishery management plan or to provide some additional assistance for side trawlers in Newfoundland?
There is a fish plant at Ramea with side trawlers, a plant at Gaultois with side trawlers, at Harbour Breton with side trawlers, and at Fortune half the trawlers are side trawlers. All of them are having these difficulties, and in Nova Scotia these conditions prevail in Louisbourg and Petit de Grat. What is going to happen?
There are four days to go before the plant at Gaultois closes, which the minister was informed on January 13 would happen. When is he going to come up with the program he promised last year for special assistance, or when is the fishery management plan going to be changed? What is the good of the 200 mile zone if it is administered so timidly, if we are going to tiptoe through the tulips and not see that our own fish plants are protected or that our own trawlers and fishermen can catch fish? What is the good of this so-called 200 mile zone? Enough of this timidity.
There are hundreds of fishermen and fish plant workers in Newfoundland in danger of being added to the already gigantic unemployment rolls in Newfoundland if the Minister of Fisheries does not act before Monday, and if the Secretary of State for External Affairs does not give him a nudge to get him acting.
Two of the Lake side trawlers went up to Labrador with assistance from the federal government last fall to try to fish on the strange grounds off Labrador. They had a disastrous trip. In ten days they caught 20,000 pounds of fish. They lost nearly all their gear fishing in those unfamiliar grounds and sustained a heavy financial loss. The wages of the crew members had to be guaranteed. Although they got a $48,000 grant from the federal government, they still lost heavily. They cannot fish in those strange grounds. They have to be permitted to fish off the south coast, off the coast of Nova Scotia and in the Gulf if those plants are going to operate this summer. What is the Minister of Fisheries doing? What is the Secretary of State for External Affairs doing? He should be worrying about the people in his own constituency just as much as he is worrying about the people of South America.
I hope the minister, who is not here tonight, will respond. I hope his parliamentary secretary will give us some indication that the fish plants on the south coast of Newfoundland will receive some special assistance to keep their side trawlers operating and their plants operating. There are at least 1,000 or 1,500 jobs involved in that area, and we cannot afford to have that unemployment added to an already fantastic unemployment rate.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Fleming (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: FISHERIES-PROPOSED PLAN FOR COMPENSATION FOR FISHERMEN ENGAGED IN REDFISH FISHERY-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of contingency plans were devised in 1976 to assist fishermen and plant operators in the event that quota restrictions or other

factors necessitated assistance over and above that available from the Temporary Assistance Program which, effective April 1, 1976, provided two cents a pound deficiency payments to trawlers and grants of six cents a pound on fillets to processors.
Data on landings, production, costs and earnings supplies by Fishing enterprises and the processing industry in connection with the assistance program have been under continuous review during the year. At the time the need for special assistance to side trawlers operating out of Newfoundland south coast plants was being evaluated the data showed that production at the Newfoundland south coast plants handling catches from side trawlers was 9 per cent higher in 1976 than in the same January to October period in 1975. When the April level of temporary assistance was established, the average landing per trip for Newfoundland side trawlers was 126,000 pounds. This catch rate was taken as an index against which succeeding months were compared, and was used to determine the need for any change in the level of assistance. The average landings varied from a high of 180,000 pounds per trip in August to 72,000 pounds per trip in October and November, with an over-all average of 125,000 pounds per trip.
Based on data compiled between April 1 and the end of October, it was concluded that total assistance provided under the Temporary Assistance program would be sufficient to offset any cash shortfalls incurred during the last three months of 1976, when the volume of landings is normally low. On the basis of evaluation of available information on landings and production for plants and side trawlers, it was concluded that additional special assistance was not justified.
We now know that during the latter part of 1976 plants remained open and fishermen continued to fish. While both production and landings were down during this period, over-all cost and earnings data for Newfoundland south coast side trawler plants show that during the period April to November inclusive, the temporary assistance program met the cash shortfalls in the industry. I might also add that there was a special financial incentive plan for vessels forced to fish outside their normal areas due to quota restrictions, and several of the Newfoundland side trawlers participated in this program.
I should like to inform you that the level of payments under the temporary assistance program, which were in effect in late 1976, are to be maintained during the first months of 1977. There is also a financial incentives plan to encourage fishing in northern non-traditional areas where Canada has substantial quotas. Conditions in the industry as a whole are being kept under continuous review, and appropriate action will be taken in response to changing circumstances in the fishing and processing sectors of the industry.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-OBJECTION TO DOCUMENTARY ON FRENCH CULTURE IN VILLAGE OF PAIN COURT
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-OBJECTION TO DOCUMENTARY ON FRENCH CULTURE IN VILLAGE OF PAIN COURT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 4 last I raised an extremely important matter in the
January 27, 1977

House with the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts). The issue was related to a documentary which appeared on CBET channel 9 on Monday, October 25, 1976, between the hours of 7 and 7.30 p.m. The documentary purported to show the French culture of the village of Pain Court. As I indicated at the time, a significant portion of the documentary dealt with an hotel, showing a stripper in the nude. When I asked the minister to investigate the matter and make an apology to the residents of the village and the township, to my astonishment the minister responded with a pompous and cavalier attitude.
The issue is not one of freedom of the press or a suggestion of editorial interference. However, when a documentary is a complete misrepresentation of the facts and reflects in a derogatory manner on the residents of a village and a township, I would have anticipated that the minister would have been more sensitive to the issue and responded in a more responsible manner.
The history of the village is contained in its name, and if the minister had reflected for a moment on that one fact the traditions and culture of the area would have unfolded before his eyes.
Pain Court is the abbreviation of the saying "Le pain est court", or "bread is scarce", which became in a sense the watchword of the early settlement which originated in about 1815. Through the years the picturesque name "Pain Court", symbolic of the early hardships of the settlement, has been resolutely retained by the people.
Their industriousness has overcome the hardships of an earlier era, resulting in a community recognized for its positive and unique contribution to the county of Kent; the area has prided itself on the strength of the family unit,the importance of high moral and ethical standards, and its people of deep religious convictions. They are recognized as having one of the finest agricultural communities in Canada and their emphasis on the importance of education has produced many prominent men and women in business, professional life and municipal affairs. I recall reviewing the cadet corps, composed of both boys and girls at the Pain Court secondary school. It is recognized as one of the finest corps in Canada; this, again, is a reflection on only one aspect of the culture of that particular community.
Sir, time does not permit me the opportunity of describing the many attributes that truly reflect the culture of Pain Court and the surrounding area. Surely it is obvious to the minister and members of the House that the documentary was an insult to the people and did not reflect the culture and traditions of the community.
As the minister also knows, I tabled in the House of Commons on November 17 last a petition containing over 400 names, which I personally signed without hesitation. Again, I have had no response to that particular petition.
Perhaps the attitude of the residents can best be described by the first of many letters I received from that area. Let me quote a portion of that letter dated October 27, 1976:
Adjournment Debate
Could you please make a thorough investigation into a program which was seen on CBET, Windsor, Channel 9 on Monday October 25, at 7 p.m. or thereabouts?
The station called it a "documentary" on Pain Court. All it was actually was free publicity for a strip joint called the Dover Hotel, which unfortunately is situated at the north end of our beautiful little village. There are so many beautiful scenes and beautiful people in the village to interview, why concentrate the major part of the program on the owner of a third class establishment and show the stripper nude ...
When word spread that there would be a documentary on the French culture in Pain Court, people flocked to the TV and had their children watch the program as well, because at 7 p.m. this is called prime time isn't it? There could not be anything objectionable on Pain Court. It is such a beautiful, peaceful sleepy little village. The people expected what was announced-French culture in the village of Pain Court. Little did they dream that they and their children would be subjected to seeing a stripper in action. Publicity of that sort only attracts undesirable riff-raff from the surrounding area. These undesirables spoil the atmosphere of Pain Court.
I recognize that this is the first time the minister has been appointed to the cabinet. I am generous enough to believe that his very flippant response to my question in the House of Commons was perhaps a reflection of his inexperience. I am also certain that, in reflecting on his initial response, the minister will not only be prepared to apologize to the residents of Pain Court in the township of Dover but will be in a position to report on my initial request for an investigation and a request for a public apology to the residents of that particular village.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REASON FOR ALLEGED SECRET EXPULSION FROM CANADA OF MR. PERDOMO, REPRESENTATIVE OFCUBA
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REASON FOR ALLEGED SECRET EXPULSION FROM CANADA OF MR. PERDOMO, REPRESENTATIVE OFCUBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief in that the information that I am seeking is very simple and to the point. It relates to my questions of this Tuesday dealing with information I have been able to obtain regarding the expulsion from Canada of certain Cuban diplomats. In order not to confuse the issue, let me make it very clear that I am not referring to the recent expulsion of the five Cubans, including three diplomats, who operated a spy school in Montreal.
I am specifically referring to the expulsion of one Alfonso Herrera Perdomo, second in command of the Cuban Embassy in Ottawa, and Rafael Reyes, an administrator officer at the Cuban Consulate in Toronto, both of whom were expelled from Canada last June without the Department of External Affairs making these expulsions public. Mr. Speaker, one must assume that either the government was trying to hide or cover up this expulsion, or that it has become the policy of the Trudeau administration not to announce the expulsion from Canada of foreign diplomats. The latter would be more in line, I suppose, since it seems to me that between the Soviets and the Cubans, expulsion of diplomats is becoming a regular habit.
It is difficult to comprehend why the government continues to tolerate and deal in good faith, as it does, with a nation that continues to show disrespect towards Canada and Canadian relations. Not only have we allowed the Cubans to operate a training camp for intelligence operations on Canadian soil, most probably under the supervision of the Soviet KGB; not only did the government close its eyes when Rafael Reyes was

organizing and supporting revolutionary left-wing Chilean refugee movements here in Canada with the hope of overthrowing the ruling Chilean government; not only does the government tolerate communist spy activities, be they Soviet or Cuban, right under its nose; not only did the Department of External Affairs allow Mr. Perdomo to negotiate with CIDA officials and employees with the hope of recruiting them as agents for the Cubans while at the same time attempting to disguise what could have been $23 million in grants and loans to that country in such a way as to make it look as though the loan was $10 million-and this, of course, is backed by the memorandum from the agency itself-but the government continues to deal with Cuba as if nothing has happened.
The aid program already consists of a $10 million loan at a nominal 3 per cent interest for a 30 year term with repayments not to begin until 1982, as well as an outright grant of $3.9 million. And this while small and medium sized businesses in Canada, operated and owned by Canadians, are virtually ignored and allowed to go bankrupt as witnessed by the highest bankruptcy rate this country has ever seen.
What I am asking the External Affairs Department to consider is the following. First, confirm the obvious, which is that Mr. Perdomo as well as Mr. Reyes were expelled from Canada while in Canada last summer. Second, inform the Canadian public whether or not the policy of the government is indeed not to make expulsions of foreign diplomats public knowledge. Third, because of the continuing disrespect shown by the Cubans toward Canadian relations, I ask that the whole matter of the Cuban aid program be brought before the sub-committee of the external affairs committee dealing with CIDA, and that all current aid programs and negotiations with that country cease until the committee has had a chance to resolve these problems.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that the parliamentary secretary does not have the authority to answer positively my reasonable requests, but perhaps he can pass them on to his minister for consideration. While I am asking him to pass things on, perhaps he could advise the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that the time has certainly come for the Prime Minister to stop shouting at the top of his lungs "Viva Cuba" and "Viva Castro" and do something positive so that we can all continue to shout "Viva Canada".

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Fleming (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REASON FOR ALLEGED SECRET EXPULSION FROM CANADA OF MR. PERDOMO, REPRESENTATIVE OFCUBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will leave editorial comment aside for the moment and simply give the response. As the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs said in replying to the questions raised by the hon. member on January 25, the recent action the government has taken regarding Cuban officials is an indication of the seriousness with which it looks at activities undertaken by representatives of any foreign government in contravention of their status in Canada. The government has applied the same principles over the years.
January 27, 1977

Last June the Canadian government requested the Cuban government to withdraw Alfonso Herrera Perdomo for activities incompatible with his diplomatic status in Canada. No other Cuban officials were involved in that case. The name of Rafael Reyes has also been mentioned in the press. In fact Reyes left Canada early in 1976 at the end of his tour of duty here. I
I can assure the House that the decision to extend aid to Cuba was based solely on the usual criteria and was not in any way influenced by what has been described by the hon. member as "deceitful practices" of any representative of any foreign government.
Adjournment Debate
More generally, hon. members on both sides of the House know very well that relations between countries may involve both good elements and, on occasion, ones that are unsatisfactory. When incidents such as this occur, it is not always advisable or in the best interests of maintaining the over-all relationship to discuss publicly and in detail the unsatisfactory problems, but rather to dispose of them quickly. The important thing is that appropriate action on any problems be taken immediately by the government, and this has been done in all such cases. These situations naturally make it more difficult to move our relations with Cuba forward as we would wish. Nevertheless, it is our intention that our over-all relations not be affected.
